speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. Is the minister now in a position to make some comment on the announcement by Dosco of a substantial reduction in the work force at their Wabana mine?

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have an answer to the question asked me in this regard last Friday by the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Tucker). The hon. member for St. John's East has, of course, indicated an interest in this matter and has conferred with me about it.
The Wabana iron ore mine of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, Limited, known as Dosco, has been a traditional supplier of medium grade iron ore to Britain and western Europe since the turn of the century. In recent years the increasing availability of competitive higher grade ores, particularly from several countries in South America and Africa, has resulted in an oversupply of ore on the world market which has cut into Canadian sales abroad including those of Dosco. In addition, the European
80	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry steel industry, and particularly that of Britain, will apparently be operating in the coming year at a level below that of 1961.
I have seen no reference to a shut-down at the Wabana mine, an expression which the hon. member for Trinity-Conception used. He also used the word "lay-off" which I believe fits better the situation involved.
While no positive statement has yet been made to my knowledge by the company about the number of miners that may be laid off, it seems highly probable that a substantial cut in the work force is contemplated and it would appear inevitable in view of present-day iron ore market conditions.
Several attempts have been made by the company in recent years with the assistance of my department to mechanize the Wabana mine and to improve the recovery and quality of the ore. Not all of these have proven successful.
To establish closer relations between overseas customers and Canadian ore producers, including Dosco, I understand that my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is considering the organization of an iron ore trade mission to Europe which would be composed of senior representatives of the iron ore industry, the Department of Trade and Commerce and my department.
May I add that Bell island has been declared a labour surplus area. The federal government therefore provides complete removal expenses for men and their families who may find employment elsewhere. May I also add that the government of Newfoundland has recently announced the construction of a trade school on the island. This school will be eligible for substantial federal government assistance under the technical-vocational training agreement which was enacted to assist in situations such as exist on Bell island.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, January 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Rodrigue Bourdages for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the adjournment I was dealing with the section of the speech from the throne that had to do with social justice. In order to commence my remarks today, I shall read that section:
Your approval will be requested for an increase in the amount of the universal old age pension payable under the Old Age Security Act, and also for legislation to increase the amount to which the federal government will contribute under the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act and the Disabled Persons Act.
When I spoke in the city of Toronto in 1957 I enunciated the new frontier policy, and so named it on behalf of the Conservative party. Following the example of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) yesterday, I will read a section of my remarks made at that time. I do not want him to have a monopoly on reading what he said on other occasions.
The Prime Minister of Ontario has just said that human betterment is of the essence of government .. .We intend to maintain all the social security measures. We intend to maintain a standard to keep pace with a rising productivity of this nation. In parliament and outside, we have condemned the meagre and niggardly assistance given to old age pensioners by the increase of 20 cents a day, which leaves them in a position where they have less purchasing power than they did in 1951. The same position applies to war pensioners and also to the retired civil servants.
At that time I felt the proper course to follow in connection with social security, particularly for older persons, was to make necessary adjustments on a cost of living basis. If that course were followed, then the amount of the increase to be given to the old age pensioners would be very, very small because one of the most remarkable contributions that has been made by this government since 1957 has been that we have been able to prevent inflation. We have been able to maintain the Canadian dollar and its purchasing power, a course which should have been adopted for several years prior to 1957 when the increase in the cost of living continued unabated to a very considerable extent.
I referred also in that speech to the war pensioners and to civil servants, and I might add by way of keeping the record clear, that this government has seen that these groups have received justice during the period we have been in office.

Now, having given the matter the very fullest consideration we have come to a conclusion, and legislation will be placed before the house. Old age pensions will be increased by $10 a month and the amount of increase we contribute to old age assistance, blind pensioners and disabled persons will be on the same basis.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

He would find that while the members of that party are loud in their protestations in the House of Commons, yet in the province of Saskatchewan, the amounts paid by way of old age assistance and other forms of assistance are less than in some other provinces throughout the country.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think we need to look too far ahead just yet. We will continue with the speech from the throne tomorrow.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

Shame. Let us make the payments. Come on.
He was referring to the acreage payments, and that brought to mind something he wants to forget, because he has adopted the attitude of speaking with authority for the farmers. However, 1 well remember the reply given by him on August 30, 1958, when we introduced the system of acreage payments. It is to be found on page 4348 of Hansard in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition who said:
We are quite sure, on this side, that the grain producers, with that problem before them, will welcome this particular assistance, will welcome this particular grant though they may be disappointed in the amount. I have no doubt that when my hon. friend from Assiniboia gets up immediately after I conclude he will call it peanuts.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I did that a couple of days ago. I shall call it a pittance today.
The hon. member now knows the extent to which the farmers of western Canada welcome the "pittance" of August, 1958 and that of January, 1962. They recognize this system is fair and is particularly helpful to the small farmers. It actually represents an amount equivalent to the two-price system being distributed, not on the bushel system, which would mean the larger farmers receiving a disproportionate amount, but in a manner that makes possible distribution among the small farmers in reasonable equality.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Last night when dealing with our wheat sales abroad I mentioned the tremendous increase that had taken place in export sales, not only in wheat but in other products. I think it should be placed on the record that concerning capital goods this government has encouraged long term financing of exports in order to ensure that we can
84	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker successfully compete in other parts of the world. This long term financing of exports of capital goods was made possible by an amendment to the Export Credits Insurance Act in 1961, which provided $200 million for that purpose. Under this legislation contracts involving export sales of $41 million worth of capital goods have been concluded, and cabinet approval has been given to provide an additional $100 million. The speech from the throne, states that the government proposes to raise the ceiling from the present figure of $200 million on total funds available to finance the export of Canadian capital goods. All these things have been beneficial to Canada and are today paying dividends as shown in the national economic recovery.
In connection with wheat and livestock in general, there has been a farm cash income from cattle 10 per cent above that of 1960. With regard to dairy products there is a problem with the surplus of butter, and this is being studied. Income from dairy products for the first nine months of the year are higher than for the corresponding period a year earlier.
The export of wheat and wheat flour last year reached the very high level of 354 million bushels. I remember that when the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill), then minister of trade and commerce, stated some years ago that 300 million bushels would be the aim, this was ridiculed by the opposition. Yet in the year 1961 we achieved a level of more than 50 million bushels beyond what was estimated at that time.
The strengthening of Canada's position as the largest seller of wheat in the commercial markets of the world has come about as a consequence of tremendous sales efforts made by various departments of the government, in particular the departments of agriculture and trade and commerce. Our traditional markets remained strong in 1961, with sales to Japan reaching a record level.
I should add that I visited Japan in response to a repeated invitation. I stayed there for a period of four or five days. There is in Japan an interest in Canada, a recognition of this country and a realization that Japan is going to continue to take its place with the free nations of the world to maintain freedom and the economic strength of each and every member of the free world.
Heavy European purchases virtually exhausted our stocks of Durum wheat. Besides the sales that were made to China providing so much employment in Vancouver and other coast ports, sales were made to Poland and Czechoslovakia. Along with these booming sales we have experienced substantial increases in price. Not many months ago the


price of wheat at Fort William was $1.67. It is now close to the international wheat agreement maximum price of $1.90. Contributing to this increase was the government's action in reducing the value of the Canadian dollar as compared with the United States dollar. This step brought about improvement in prices generally for agricultural products for export and increased the opportunities for Canadians to export. Further, no effort has been spared to lessen the effects of the severe drought in the west during the past year.
With regard to the payments estimated for 1961, cash farm income was $2.9 billion; realized gross income, $3.3 billion; realized net income $1.4 billion. These are all slightly above the corresponding figures for 1960 in spite of the sharply reduced output on the prairies.
I thought I ought to make reference to the agricultural situation, which was another matter to which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) did not refer. I am sure that as he travelled across Canada in his pilgrimages, he found everywhere appreciation for what this government has done to maintain agricultural prices in all parts of our country.
As I listened to the hon. gentleman yesterday I began to look back a few months. I looked back to that gathering of the seers in Kingston in September, 1960. That was a gathering to which I think more and more attention will be paid than in the past. I repeat that the slogan for the election, whenever it comes, is "The Liberals have the answer".

speechtext: I want to recall this because I know my hon. friends opposite do not want to hear about this conference. I intend to refer to it in some particular because those who were the heads of that conference, those who expressed themselves at that conference, are now the cornerstone of this hew temple, the new Liberals who allegedly have the answer. The chairman was Walter Gordon.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I thought they were the same old gang. Make up your mind.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Then there were the various committees:	Maurice Lamontagne,
unemployment, fiscal policy, monetary policy; Mitchell Sharp, foreign policy; C. M. Drury, vice chairman; T. W. Kent, vice chairman. This is quite an interesting gathering. All these people are now receiving more than usual attention from the leadership of the Liberal party.
They gathered together there. Hon. gentlemen opposite speak about circuses. I think of that gathering at Kingston as the circus of the bureaucrats. The gathering of those who today are in the leadership of the Liberal party includes the very same people who in the days of war and from 1945 on paralysed parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They paralysed parliament and interfered with the rights of the provinces. They believe that desirable economic objectives can only be attained by turning a nation into a disciplined and controlled unit. They believe that the principles they followed in the days of war and under those so-called emergency legislation enactments following the war are once more to be imposed upon the Canadian people.
I am going to refer in particular to quotations from the statements they made. We do not accept those principles. We have not lost, as they have, our belief in democracy. We believe that changes must take place; that they should be within the framework of the constitution and without invading that constitution. Some of the recommendations that were made at that conference would once more require the implementation of emergency legislation in Canada depriving the provinces of their rights and invading the jurisdiction of the provinces.
I think of these people. I am not going to name them all, but most will be able to identify those who treated parliament with patent and unconcealed contempt and deprived it of its rights, those men referred to as bureaucrats in a previous government. They were our masters. That is what we fought against year after year in this House of Commons. These are the men who want that power again and they have made it clear that they are ready to act in accordance with the statements they have made. These are the men who bypassed parliament, the men who found it easier to rule by order in council under so-called emergency legislation. These are the men represented by the statement made in the House of Commons on April 21, 1953 by the minister of trade and
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker commerce of that day, whose deputy minister was Mitchell Sharp-"If we have overstepped our powers I make no apology for doing so". These are the bright bureaucratic boys. These were the dictators who dominated Canada. I shall refer, as well, to some of those recently acquired and the views which they expressed at that particular time.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) spoke yesterday as he always does about mumble and jumble and disorganization. I notice that Mr. Drury was one of this distinguished group. He was deputy minister of defence when Mr. Currie made his report. That report was made, it will be recalled, in 1953 and this is what Mr. Currie said:
The conclusion I have come to is that while there has been a general breakdown in the system of administration, supervision and accounting-
"A general breakdown". This is one of the pilots of Liberalism of today. He said there had been a general breakdown in the system of administration, supervision and accounting in the whole department of defence. Then the report adds this:
-it was only at Petawawa that extensive irregularities over a prolonged period of time took place.
I intend to refer now-not because I do not want to see outstanding men desirous of coming into public life-to some of them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Don't smear them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Everyone wants to see the best come into public life, but it is a strange, strange thing, this agglomeration, this grouping. You can see it forming every day. They had the answers in 1945-1957. It is the same old bunch. When I read that the Leader of the Opposition describes his party as the new Liberal party I look over and see the same old faces that were there in the old party. In the advertising, or in the resolutions, they are referred to now as the new Liberal party. Why is that? I suppose it is the sting of conscience. I ordinarily would refer here to those who constitute the philosophical wing were it not for the fact that the philosophical wing appears now to be in control.
I should refer first to Mr. Lamontagne. He is also a candidate. He made a speech at Kingston, and I intend to give the Leader of the Opposition an opportunity again to say whether or not he agrees with the views of his advisers-views which have been revealed so clearly at that conference and since. Mr. Lamontagne made a certain statement, and I have the quotation here. He advocated rigid state controls to achieve the triple objective of the Liberal party. Controls, and it could be done. That was the Lamontagne

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker thesis. The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, a paper which has certainly never been one of our major supporters, said of this:
A government sworn to all three objectives would need to rule with whips and scorpions.
So this is the new philosophy. The Hamilton Spectator said this was "back door socialism". That may be the reason why the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is reported as having ambitions to join with some of the hon. gentlemen who are now sitting opposite me.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
After all-and the hon. member for Assiniboia is always most congenial-when his own party will not use the word "socialism" any more he is bound to go to some who hold that view.
Then the Quebec Chronicle-Telegraph said of those remarks of Mr. Lamontagne:
That lecture would have been worth its weight in gold to Fidel Castro.
These are the views which are broadcast across Canada. I intend to quote the references because these are the men who were in the background before. Now they are in the foreground. These are the philosophers, and we want to know the extent to which advisers who hold these views are listened to when they give advice. The Ottawa Journal had this to say about it:
The refrain which ran all through the Kingston conclave was the refrain of the state as a shepherd.
Among other things I have a list here of what is proposed. There is the price board. I ask the Leader of the Opposition whether he believes in this price control board, this so-called conciliation board. Is this the way in which the Liberals are going to control the economy of Canada?
The determination of monetary policy and the management of the public debt should be divorced.
A special and permanent price conciliation board could be set up or this task could be assigned to an enlarged and stronger restrictive trade practices commission. It is desirable that those who enjoy special monopolistic controls within our so-called free and competitive system be submitted to a scheme of public supervision. Moreover, such a scheme appears necessary if we really want to prevent market power inflation and the unfair distribution of the national income which it creates.
I ask the Leader of the Opposition: are these the views of Mr. Lamontagne, an adviser today of the first rank? Do they represent the kind of Canada that the Liberal party would bring into being if it should obtain power; or are these just statements that were made for the information of the assembled conclave, not intended to be carried into effect? What are some of the views? The Victoria daily Times is not a
[Mr. Diefenbaker.!
paper that is regularly antipathetic to the Liberal party, and in an editorial it has this to say with reference to this speech:
-his speech at a recent unofficial conference of liberally-minded Canadians . . . does not represent Liberal party policy.
Then it goes on to say:
It seems unlikely that the Liberal party is ready to embrace what can only be considered a repudiation of its basic philosophy and its policy in office.
. . . The board's ruling would not be final, a price increase could be effected even over the board's objection, but the intention of the device is to concentrate the power of the state and of public opinion against the increase. This is state control of prices by indirection and inevitably would lead in the end to direct control.
The Winnipeg Tribune points out the same situation. I am not going into detail but it says that this is a serious matter. Even the Winnipeg Free Press could not swallow this doctrine. It had this to say:
The power to legislate with regard to prices has a history which is of general interest in view of the proposal by Mr. Maurice Lamontagne at the recent conference of Liberals at Queen's University.
Then it says this:
Price fixing by governments must inevitably lead to confusion, uncertainty and inefficiency.
The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix says: Disagreement continues to mount over certain policies and proposals advocated at the conference of liberally-minded individuals ... A proposal made by Professor Maurice Lamontagne, economic adviser to Liberal leader L. B. Pearson, has evoked strong opposition. Mr. Lamontagne's proposal included the establishment of a federal board which would approve or oppose price increases by monopolies.
Then it says:
Apart from the fact that Mr. Lamontagne's proposal contravenes long-established Liberal policy-
That may be the reason for calling themselves the new Liberal party now.
-it points up the way in which the so-called "ginger group" . . . would dictate Liberal policy.
That is the dream of Mr. Lamontagne. The Winnipeg Free Press said: this proposal means an attempt by the federal government to regulate so-called monopolies with regard to prices. The Quebec Chronicle-Telegraph takes the same view and says that this is a policy that is contrary to the principles of free enterprise and a denial of the principles of old Liberalism. Well, that is not all. Mr. Lamontagne occupies a central position and no doubt will be able to expound these doctrines in the days ahead.
Recently, however, there was another acquisition, Mr. Tom Kent, a very fine gentleman. He is a special assistant. I wonder whether he has the answers. I know that when the Leader of the Opposition appointed him he said, "he will serve in an anonymous and inarticulate capacity". Mr. Lamontagne

was not in that position. Mr. Kent has the answers, 67 pages of them, which he placed before this conference. If his doctrine is not acceptable, why is it that he is taken into the family as an adviser? I do not have to make any observations about it. The Regina Leader-Post said this:
. . . the inarticulate Mr. Kent has already acquired considerable prominence for his radical views and for his advocacy of planning and restrictions imposed on business by government. In his silent service behind the Liberal throne, the assumption is Mr. Kent will attempt to mould Liberal policies to conform with his personal views. This cannot be other than disturbing to many faithful followers of the Liberal party.
I understand that. That is why it is new. The new Liberal party has the answers.
Their Liberalism has moved a long way from outmoded laissez faire concepts. They acknowledge the state has a role to play in safeguarding the public from abuses in our private enterprise economy. But their thinking has not reached the extreme position held by Mr. Kent that private business and the corporations are speeding to their doom and desperately need rescuing through government intervention.
I am going to give the Leader of the Opposition an opportunity to clarify this matter so that we will understand exactly the degree to which these views constitute the reason for the program, "The Liberals Have the Answer", which is being distributed across Canada.
Mr. Kent pointed to expenditures "on advertising and merchandising generally" for immediate government scrutiny.
He is going to get all the papers in Canada under his control.
While not enlarging on what "merchandizing generally" covered-
I am still quoting from the Regina Leader-Post which is often quoted as a model of correctness.
-he singled out advertising, proposing that by stages expenditures in this category become nondeductible for income tax purposes. Later, he hedged somewhat in declaring he did not pretend to complete certainty that "this is the right thing to do." But he added he was "quite sure that it would yield great benefits" in averting the present alleged waste of money and talents in the stimulation of "unimportant wants."
Is that the Liberal party concept?
Mr. Kent evidently is among those who would save the people from their own follies in spending their money as they desire. He suggested that with less spent on "unimportant wants"-
That is, advertising, merchandising.
-there would be more money "for schools and the rest." This, in turn, suggests the tax collector will gather the money the people cease to spend foolishly for use "for schools and the rest."
Mr. Kent expressed the somewhat arresting view that since advertising expenses are deductible before profits are determined, the government in effect is subsidizing advertising.
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
I want to give the Leader of the Opposition this chance. Are the views of Mr. Lamon-tagne and Mr. Kent the views of the new Liberal party? Does he accept them? I am going to be very reasonable. He can pick whichever horn of the dilemma he wants. He can pick the most comfortable of these two horns. Let me read on.
To one holding Mr. Kent's views, it would be but a short hop into a socialized state.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I see a smile on the face of the house leader of the N.D.P., and there is reason for that smile. Listen to the next sentence.
It seems that Mr. Kent would be more at home as a consultant to a party other than the Liberal party.
I am going to read some excerpts from this philosophy, for this was a gathering of the erstwhile bureaucrats of the war period and the period immediately thereafter and others variously gathered together. These are some of the ideas. Would there be any increase in social security if Mr. Kent had anything to do with it? I refer to page 39, and this is a long statement, Mr. Speaker. This is what he says:
The measures I have suggested do not include any increase in general social payments such as family allowances and pensions. If we are to maintain that exclusion, as I believe we should, because other measures are far more urgent-we must recognize that there are many welfare problems hardly touched.
Then he comes out with his views about taxes. The Leader of the Opposition says that taxes are too high. May I say that there are 75,000 Canadians paying less income tax today than they were paying when we came into office.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Seventy five per cent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Get the facts straight.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am grateful for the assistance of hon. gentlemen opposite. Seventy five per cent of Canadian income taxpayers are paying less today than they were paying when this government came into office. I speak to the Leader of the Opposition through you, Mr. Speaker, and remind him of the words-the wise words, as I think they were once referred to by the Leader of the Opposition-of Mr. Kent. Let me read what he has to say about taxation:
I am not, of course, arguing that we owe all this to high taxes . . . But the fact is that high taxes have not prevented an economic performance that is, by all previous standards, good.
That was in September, 1960.
The burden of proof is on those who claim that taxes at the present level do economic damage, compared with what would happen if governments

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker spent less and individuals were able to spend more ... It follows that, while a sharp rise in tax rates certainly has some "disincentive" effect at first, it will weaken, not strengthen, as people grow accustomed to the new tax levels.
This is the philosophy of the new Liberal party, the Liberal party that, it is said, has the answer.
It is hard, in other words, to see that taxation at the levels to which we are now accustomed exercises any large restraining influence on economic activities.
I simply quote these observations by way of answer to some of the statements that were made by the hon. gentleman. The quotation continues:
In short, the conventional arguments about the anti-productive effects of taxation are unacceptable.
Then he goes on to say this:
We have, in other words, to ensure that our economy does in fact work successfully-fairly, efficiently, inventively-while sustaining a bigger tax burden.
Is that the new Liberal party policy? Is that the answer they have? Then he comes out with this idea. The people across Canada will be interested to learn that the chief adviser to the Leader of the Opposition who has now been taken unto his bosom in an even closer relationship, said this:
The major step to greater equality lies, however, in steeper taxation of inheritances.
Is that the new Liberal answer? Is that what is meant when it is said that the Liberal party has the answer? Then he explains the statement:
There is no justification for such large inequalities of opportunity as survive our present succession duties and gift taxes.
Is that one of the answers they have? He continues:
The proper basis of taxation is, I suggest, the individual's total receipts, in inheritance and gifts, from one source or several; and beyond some modest total, they should be taxed on a considerably steeper scale than now operates.
I again give the Leader of the Opposition the opportunity of saying whether this is the philosophy of the new Liberal party. If not, I cannot understand the appointment of advisers who hold to doctrines that are so economically difficult to accept.
Then we come to advertising:
The only solution-
Everything is swept away there.
-therefore lies through public policy. It is the proper role of government to step in and alter the incentives-not to interfere and lay down detailed instructions about what should be done or not done, but simply to make advertising less attractive.
What is this doctrine enunciated by a man who has occupied such positions as the editorship of the Free Press'? Is this the doctrine that we are to have placed before the people

of Canada or is it going to be kept in the background? I think one can guess the answer to that question. He states further:
In principle, there is no reason why advertising should not be taxed, like liquor or gasoline or thousands of other useful things . . . the better first approach probably is to refuse to allow advertising, and perhaps other merchandising expenditures, for tax purposes.
Here in my hand I hold material bearing the slogan "The Liberals have the answer". I hope the Leader of the Opposition will tell us the degree to which he, Mr. Kent, and Mr. Lamontagne diverge. This is strange doctrine. We continue on from there. If we get away from allowing advertising as a deduction, these are the great results that will follow:
If, for example, we did reduce advertising, it would thereby become easier also to raise existing taxes on consumption-liquor revenues, gas tax, vehicle licences, real property taxes, and general sales tax.
Do you see the unveiling of this remarkable economic charter of Canada's Liberalism? If we did this we would be able to increase liquor revenue, gas taxes and finally the sales tax. Then he continues:
Our provincial premiers could better have their day.
Then he goes on to say this:
Having mentioned property taxes, which so closely affect the most poverty stricken of our three levels of government, I would say that here increases seem very reasonable.
Then he finally sums it all up in this way:
While a general capital gains tax has many undesirable features, and certainly is not to be preferred to increased taxation of inheritance, there is a very great deal to be said for a specific tax on increments in property values.
Is that the new financial direction of the new Liberal party? I could give a number of quotations with regard to this matter but I do not think it is necessary. I have simply placed before you, Mr. Speaker, the basic doctrine and the basic supports that stand behind the Leader of the Opposition and his advisers who daily or regularly place these views before him. Speaking of circuses, may I say that I wish to see the Leader of the Opposition perform. Does he accept the views of Mr. Lamontagne and of Mr. Kent? Again I give him a choice. He can say yes or he can say no. That will be a performance compared with which the acrobatics exhibition one could see in any circus would appear most modest. I hope the Leader of the Opposition will reply at the earliest opportunity.

speechtext: These views are economic nonsense. That is all they are.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime
Minister has, in his somewhat agitated and personal attack on certain persons who cannot defend themselves in this house, asked me a question. I am asking him if he would like an answer to the question now?

speechtext: I was asked certain questions about statements expressed by individuals at a conference at Queen's University some years ago. The Prime Minister, being the head of the Tory government, will have a very difficult time understanding, but this congress-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I want to answer the question. I said the Prime Minister may have difficulty in understanding this, but at this conference it was made clear that there would be a free, open and full discussion and the people would be speaking there in their individual, personal capacities. Therefore-sit down, Mr. Prime Minister, sit down -it would be just as foolish for the Prime Minister to assume that those who made statements at that conference were speaking -be calm, sir-that those who were speaking at that time were laying down policies for the Liberal party as it would be for me to assume that Mr. John Fisher, in his statements in earlier years, was reflecting the views of the Tory government today.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I have been waiting for an answer. He would not answer the question. How could he answer it and not accept people with doctrines which he does not uphold, because he is afraid to say he agrees with them. These people have become the philosophic segment of the Liberal party and the advisers to the Leader of the Opposition. They were appointed, at least Mr. Kent was, since they expounded these views. The answer of the Leader of the Opposition makes it clear what the situation is. In spite of the views that they hold and held and declared, he says they do not necessarily represent his views but he appoints them as advisers. About what are they advising him? Why get advice on matters which you are not going to accept? I leave it to the common sense of the house and the country to answer that question. Now, we begin to see something of the meaning of the new Liberal party.

Now then, Mr. Speaker, I come to one other matter and that is the prophecies the Leader of the Opposition has made. You know, he is a man of tremendous defiance. In 1958, he said "Bring on the election; the sooner the better". Then, when we brought it on he said, "Well, I did not expect you to do that."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why are you always looking back? Look ahead.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

I want to read some of the predictions in 1958-"by their words you shall judge them". Speaking in Vancouver in February, 1958, he said:
The Liberal party is going to make gains in every province.
If they come as close next time as after these prophecies that were being made, we will be quite satisfied. On February 22, 1958, at Cobourg, the Leader of the Opposition was asked to forecast the next federal cabinet. He said, "All I can tell you is it will be Liberal." Then, on March 26, we find this quotation in the Toronto Globe and Mail:
In the past two weeks there has been a great change in public opinion in favour of the Liberals.
A little later he said:
I have found a great revival in the party, a new spirit of energy and enthusiasm ... we have a future.
They also have a past. At another point, he
said:
I have been stimulated and encouraged by what can only be called a revival of Liberalism.
On November 6, 1957, he said:
The Liberal party has nothing to worry about in facing the voters in the next dominion election.
Then, when they are talking about the situation in one province, Quebec, it is well to go back to see what they were saying. I am not going to mention the prophecies of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) with regard to Saskatchewan. I have them here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am being overlooked.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

I want to mention the prophecies with regard to Quebec because the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) makes prophecies regularly. About two weeks

The Address-Mr. Diefenhaker before the election the hon. member for Essex East was at Westmount. I do not know whether or not he had any of the frontbenchers with him at that time. speechtext: I have had the opportunity on former occasions, Mr. Speaker, to follow the Prime Minister in the throne speech debate and have often wondered what hour I might get in. speechtext:
But, so far as setting forth an economic program for the full development of Canadian resources, it has been the most barren. Our country has stagnated under the Conservative government in the last few years, and there has been more unemployment in this post-war period than in any similar period since the end of the war. We have already had statistics placed on the record showing by way of real per capita income how our country has been standing still, and in some years slipping backwards.
If one relates the loss of any increase in real incomes in Canada, then I would suggest that on a per capita basis Canadians have been losing at least $40 to $50 per year in incomes each and every year that this government has been in office. In 1957 real per capita purchasing power in Canada, based on constant 1949 dollars was $1,437. In the next year, 1958, this had dropped to $1,414, a decrease of $23. The year 1959 was almost the same, with more stagnation, more marking down, more indecision and ineffectiveness on the part of the government. Per capita income then was just $1,426, a meagre increase of $12, and in 1960 it was $1,425, a drop of $1 per person in real per capita purchasing power. The figures for 1961 are not available but the change in the gross national product, which would indicate an increase of some 1.3 per cent in real incomes, is still inadequate and is a very small increase in the real standards of living.
Before the Conservative government took office one heard criticism from time to time by working people that they were paying too much into the unemployment insurance fund, and they were objecting to paying into a fund that seemed to be getting larger and larger and larger. They asked why they should contribute to it since it always seemed to be growing; but now that criticism has ended. When this government came into office the fund began to wither away. So much unemployment created such a tremendous drain on the fund

that a surplus of $926 million on December 31, 1956, is apparently in imminent danger of being wiped out altogether.
What does the government say about this. In the throne speech it is stated:
My government will also ask you to appropriate monies required in the unemployment insurance fund to safeguard the rights of workers until the report of the special committee inquiring into the unemployment insurance program has been received and can be acted upon.
That is an indication of a further $1 billion cost by this government to the people of Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has followed a regular procedure since taking office in allowing the Governor General the most meagre latitude in presenting the speech from the throne, after which the Prime Minister comes into the house and, day after day, speech after speech, does his best to garner the greatest possible amount of publicity. This year has been no exception. The Prime Minister has been doing it in stages. He was able to get in his prepared text last night before six o'clock and thus was able to scoop the news. He was able to get in more announcements in the evening and also some announcements this morning, but what he did not tell us is by what means the Canadian economy will be called upon to meet the many worth-while expenditures which he has announced.
He has given us one side of the financial ledger. He has said these are some of the expenditures his government is recommending. I am not objecting to the expenditures; I am in favour of them, but he has not been candid with the Canadian people when he has not told us how these expenditures in general would be met. One would expect the Minister of Finance to do so in a budget, and I suggest this government owes it to the Canadian people to present a budget in this parliament before an election is announced.
We are in favour of the legislation that the Prime Minister has announced and which is designed to bring about certain improvements which we have advocated for many years, and we are prepared today, tomorrow, and for the balance of the eight-day throne speech debate to set aside the regular business of the house so that we can go ahead with some of the measures that have been announced.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) decides when the election will be held. We suggest that the legislation that has been forecast should be presented to parliament immediately so that the Canadian people will be assured that these measures are on the statute books.
We suggest further that the government should present its budget. When it has
The Address-Mr. Argue presented the legislation forecast and the budget, we shall then welcome an election or as soon thereafter as the government may care to call it. But we do not want any repetition of promises. We feel the Canadian public have a right to know how the moneys will be raised to meet the many important expenditures that are being announced.
Much has been said in this debate about Canada's position in external trade and the handling of the discussions with the United Kingdom surrounding the United Kingdom's proposal to join the European common market. Two different approaches have been taken. One thing is certain, the United Kingdom's plan to join the European common market does bring into very serious question the ability of Canada to hold the United Kingdom market for important products in the years ahead.
I have a publication here credited to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) and circulated through his department. It points out that the European common market will have very high tariffs against many Canadian products-a tariff against Canadian wheat of 20 per cent; against flour of 30 per cent; against tobacco of 30 per cent; against plywood of 15 per cent; against maple flooring of 10 per cent, and so on, right through many products that are most important to Canada's welfare.
This is the context in which the government is negotiating with the United Kingdom with regard to its entry into the European common market. We do not know what the outcome of these negotiations will be. We feel that it does in fact threaten the economic future of the Canadian nation. We feel there has to be some association of Canada with the European common market so that this huge market, this market of western nations, this market where standards of living are increasing, will be available to Canadian products.
We point out strongly that Canada had an opportunity in October, 1957 to do something about this question of our success in holding the United Kingdom market, when the free trade offer to Canada was made by the United Kingdom. We had a chance then to get into a common market between the United Kingdom and Canada. We had a chance then to secure the market in the United Kingdom for Canadian products. This government muffed the chance. This government failed. This government was too shortsighted to enunciate a policy. Following this, Britain has come to the conclusion that it has no choice but to join the European common market. Whatever serious repercussions may follow for Canadian trade, much of the blame can be laid at the doorstep of this administration which

The Address-Mr. Argue failed to take appropriate action when the far reaching proposal of a free trade area between the United Kingdom and Canada was made.
There are many things in the speech from the throne with which we agree. There are many things that need further clarification. There is one statement which reads as follows:
My government will ask you to take steps to ensure that the forthcoming redistribution of electoral districts is made in an equitable manner upon an objective basis.
We have heard a great deal about independent bodies. I take it the Prime Minister is suggesting that the method for the redistribution of seats in the House of Commons will be taken out of the hands of the House of Commons and given, at least in the first stages, to a so-called independent body. Let us hope it is independent. Let us hope it is not loaded with a bunch of Tory politicians. It is fine to say we are going to have an independent body. We shall look at the personnel of the independent body when it is appointed and if we think it is independent, we shall be pleased.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that if he wants an independent body he should have consultation with the other political parties in this country to try to work out an approved board or commission which will not be merely a plaything or in danger of being a plaything of the government, but will in fact have the confidence of the members of all parties in the house.

We hear a great deal about national unity and it behoves all of us in the House of Commons to do everything we can to bring about

a sense of national unity and of national purpose in this country. We would be blind if we did not realize that in the province of Quebec there are important sections which feel they should go the whole way by becoming a separate nation and withdrawing from confederation, which in my judgment has proven so successful in most respects over the years.
What is this government doing to suggest to the people of Quebec, to those whose mother tongue is French, that they have equal rights in our nation? I cannot say whether there is anything in the press reports that there was a paragraph in the speech from the throne that was to make the announcement that legislation would be brought in to provide bilingual cheques. It is said by the people in Quebec who take rather extreme views on certain of these questions that this will do very little to bring about their renewed confidence in confederation. That may be right. But why hesitate on a small matter-if this is a relatively small matter-with regard to the things necessary to bring about greater unity in our country? Parliament passed a bill on second reading on January 31, 1958 to provide for this, with only nine members opposing it. Is it significant that every single one was a Conservative? Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for the luncheon recess I was saying that the government had not moved forward in such a way as to give proper recognition of the bicultural nature of this country. The journey of the cabinet to Quebec city has already been highlighted in this debate. Very little came of that journey. One of the things that Canadians looked for was a recognition by the Prime Minister that members of the cabinet from the province of Quebec should take a more leading role. Consider the representation from the province of Quebec in this cabinet. We find one cabinet minister in the front row and five in the second. With the possible exception of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer), who is not known to be particularly close to the Prime Minister, the people of the province of Quebec see their ministers in possession of very junior portfolios. I suggest this is one of the ways in which the Prime Minister has failed to give

proper recognition to the people of Quebec and to the bicultural and bilingual nature of our country.
The Prime Minister announced this morning that we are to see some increase in the old age pensions-an increase of $10 a month. That is welcome. It is long overdue. The policy of this party in this regard is clear. We say the minimum pension should be $75 a month and that on the basis of this minimum should be built up an adequate pension system. We thought this was perhaps what the government had in mind but it appears from the letter addressed to the premier of Ontario, which was tabled, that the government does not have in mind a general, comprehensive old age retirement plan but rather a plan in which a further means test will be used-a plan which will not embrace in any way those who are now covered by private pensions. We shall have some further remarks to make on this subject if and when the government gives us the advantage of seeing this legislation. As we see it now from the details contained in the letter, it would appear to be inadequate in many respects.
We regret that at this session the government has failed to move forward in the field of health insurance. I have an amendment which I wish to move at the conclusion of my remarks and this will make it clear that we feel the government should be moving forward to provide a prepaid medical care program for Canadians.
The Prime Minister spent some time dealing with the government's program for agriculture. He repeated time and time again in his presentation that the government program for agriculture was designed to assist the small farmer. I suggest that the general, overall program for agriculture is inadequate. It is hesitant and it does nothing to help farmers even small farmers in any particular fashion. I ask the Prime Minister: where are the deficiency payments for hogs? These were promised. We even had legislation. Where are the deficiency payments for eggs? The last was made in the fall of 1960. Egg prices have been scandalously low and still are scandalously low. Many farmers have marketed hogs and obtained prices less than the government's stated prices. What the government has done, through the Agricultural Prices Support Act, is to place these products on the open market and let the prices go as low as the market will allow. Where is the support price for poultry? There is no effective support price for hogs, eggs or poultry yet these are the products which many small farmers produce and in respect of which they desire support by way of price stabilization.
How does the government's program to take feed grain away from the wheat board 26207-1-7
The Address-Mr. Argue help small farmers? It has, in fact, worked to the detriment of small farmers by making it impossible for the wheat board to control the sale of feed grains. As far as all farmers are concerned, this government is following the same course as it has in so many other fields-a lot of legislation, a lot of words, a lot of window dressing but very little by way of real benefit.
The Prime Minister says we are going to get some acreage payments. The day parliament opened he said he wanted the debate on the speech from the throne set aside at an early date. Then he talked for two days. We could have dealt with this matter yesterday, but he was talking. We could have taken it today, but he was still talking. He has not even said he would act tomorrow. Apparently he has changed his mind; he thinks there is no hurry now. The speech from the throne says that these payments are to be made because there was a drought. The matter is put in these words:
The drought in the prairie provinces during 1961 has resulted in severe losses, however, and you will he asked to provide assistance by means of acreage payments to the farmers who have been affected.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) comes into the house and in the light of the statement in the speech from the throne says that the acreage payments are to be in compensation for a two price system. Which is it? Or should I venture to suggest that there are going to be two acreage payments? There should be, one because there has been a drought-that is what the speech from the throne says-and the other because there should be compensation for the low price of wheat going into the domestic market.
The drought did not happen this winter; it happened last summer. The Prime Minister went out to check on the crop situation. He flew out and landed somewhere in northern Saskatchewan. He apparently looked at one or two crops of wheat and he issued a statement. He said that he was very pleased that crop conditions were not nearly as bad as he had expected. He landed where there was a crop but he did not go to the southern part the province where, throughout many areas, the yield was zero. There was no crop at all.
He sent the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) out a little later to check on the crop. Where did he go? He landed at Riceton and the television cameras were there, these press and television people who never look after the Minister of Agriculture according to the minister. They were right with him. They went to the farm of Gordon Brown of Riceton and the minister had his picture taken, in a dry area where many farmers had no crop, in front of a 20,000 bushel pile of wheat.

The Address-Mr. Argue This tremendous publicity was spread across Canada. I am sure a lot of people in eastern Canada thought that the farmers of western Canada were simply crying once again and said to themselves, "Look at the great crop". Because the weather was hot the Minister of Agriculture had his picture taken with his shirt off. He may lose more than his shirt in the weeks ahead, but all this was very misleading propaganda.
The Minister of Agriculture then said and the Prime Minister agreed that the reason for not making acreage payments then was that the wheat board machinery was so busy turning out cheques for the farmers. If you want a laugh, that is all you have to tell the farmers. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture did not say as they should have that the wheat board could not print the cheques because there was no money. Surely it is a fundamental principle of parliamentary control of the purse that parliament has to vote the money first whether or not the machinery to print the cheques is working. Parliament was not asked last fall to provide the money. The Minister of Agriculture says that the machinery has broken down.

speechtext:
The machinery might have worked overtime. The truth is, Mr. Speaker, that here we have more misleading statements and further lack of action. Belatedly the Prime Minister now says, "We will do it; we will set aside the business of the house". The opposition say, "fine, let us do it immediately", but last night the leader of the house said, "Well, there is time; we will do it later".
We want action in this field and we want it now. I suggest that there should be a further and substantial increase in prairie farm assistance payments to compensate for crop failure, as well as the acreage payments to which the Prime Minister has referred.
The government takes credit for selling a lot of wheat and a lot of wheat has been sold. But other countries are doing fairly well too. Australia has been selling wheat to China. From December 1, 1960, to October 28, 1961, Australia sold 71 million bushels of wheat to China. In a much longer period, Canada sold 51 million bushels of wheat to China. Australia has done better. In the case of India, Australia sold 14 million bushels of wheat within that period of time while in the last crop year Canada sold less than 4 million bushels.
In the face of this kind of record the Minister of Agriculture was in Rome and he was going to go to the iron curtain countries. It has already been placed on the record by


Victor Mackie of the Winnipeg Free Press that the Minister of Agriculture said he did not have time to sell any wheat because the Prime Minister wanted him to come home and go out on the hustings to make political campaign speeches across the country.
China has not bought any flour under the agreement. When some of us suggested that this was not a firm contract the government said, "Certainly it is a firm contract; China will take it". But China has not taken any flour. Mr. Mackie quotes the Minister of Agriculture as using these words:
It is our attitude that there is no breach of contract by the Chinese if they do not take flour.
In other words, there would be no breach of contract if they did not take anything, because there was no contract. It was merely an exchange of letters which would result in a sale of wheat if the price is right, if we have the wheat, and if China wants it. There is a great job to be done in continuing to sell our wheat and I suggest that the Prime Minister would have been much better advised if he had allowed the Minister of Agriculture to go behind the iron curtain to continue to try to sell more wheat even to iron curtain countries, even to countries to which this government provides no diplomatic recognition.
What is the government doing for the small farmers? They said they were going to do a great deal. So far we have had no acreage payments. So far the debate on the speech from the throne has not been set aside to provide such payments. They say they have protected the farmers by their crop insurance scheme. In 1961 because of the drought net income from agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan fell to $122 million from $354 million, a drop of two thirds in one year because of the crop failure.
Where is the crop insurance plan? Oh, it is on the statute books. You can read it. It is there. It sounds good but very few farmers are able to afford it. The rates are too high. In the province of Manitoba about 25 per cent of the farmers are under the scheme. In Saskatchewan only 197 farmers out of
100,000	felt last year that they could afford the premiums under the act. There is little possibility of this legislation being used in any comprehensive way unless further and substantial amendments are made by the government so that the premiums may be reduced and so that there will be a reinsurance feature in order that in a time of widespread crop failure the costs may be borne not merely by provincial governments but also in some measure by the federal

government. We have had a lot of window dressing and a lot of things are being said, but not much is being done.
We had a controversy in the house last year, Mr. Speaker, about a certain pamphlet printed by the Department of Agriculture entitled "ARDA". It was distributed before the legislation was passed by the house. It was such a wonderful program that they distributed the literature on it early. The resolution was presented in the house on December 15, 1960. The minister was going to act. He was in a hurry. On May 22, 1961, he said, as found on page 5195 of Hansard:
-I hope in this year 1961, a minimum of at least one tentative agreement in each province for at least one pilot area and, I hope, several in each province.
My information is that not one agreement has been signed, not one.

But the literature is printed and propaganda is spread across the country. speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to follow the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in congratulating the mover (Mr. Bour-dages) and the seconder (Mr. Browne, Van-couver-Kingsway), of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I feel sure that all hon. members of the house will agree that they did an excellent job. They spoke clearly, concisely and objectively. I am sure that the people in their constituencies will feel as proud of them as we who are members of the same party felt of them on Friday afternoon.
Judging by the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. party, there is a distinct lack of knowledge on the part of the opposition with regard to the soundness of the Canadian economy today, and of our economic prospects for this year which we are just entering. Hence I thought that I should like to take a few minutes of the time of the house, Mr. Speaker, in order to speak about economic matters under five headings, namely
(1) economic indicators which show the progress which our economy has made during the past year; (2) what the government has done, and is doing, to assist our producers; (3) Britain's negotiations for entering the common market; (4) the progress which our economy has made since we formed the government in 1957; and (5) the economic outlook for 1962.
First of all, then, I should like to speak about the economic indicators which show where our economy has been going during the past year. The figures I shall quote are from the dominion bureau of statistics, and in every case are the latest figures available from the bureau.
1.	Gross National Product: In the third quarter of 1961, the gross national product

The Address-Mr. Hees reached a high of $37.4 billion on a seasonally adjusted basis. This was an increase of nearly $1 billion from its second quarter level, and represents a gain of 4 per cent over the same period a year earlier.
2.	Consumer Spending: Consumer spending continued upward during the past year, and in the third quarter, was 4 per cent higher than in the third quarter a year ago.
3.	Exports: Exports of goods and services advanced at an accelerated pace during the past year, rising by 2 per cent from the first to the second quarter, and by 6 per cent from the second to the third quarter. As the Prime Minister pointed out in his very eloquent and able presentation to the house, merchandise exports for the first ten months of the year showed an increase of 7.2 per cent from the same period a year earlier. In the latest three months comparison, the increase was twice as great, namely 14 per cent.
4.	Industrial Production:	A substantial
advance has taken place in industrial production since March of 1961, and during the last three months for which figures are available- August, September and October-the index of industrial production was 6 per cent higher than a year earlier.
5.	Personal Incomes: The trend in total personal income gathered strength as the pace of business quickened during the year. Following a moderate increase in the second quarter, personal income moved up strongly in the third quarter and reached a level 4 per cent higher than in the third quarter a year ago.
6.	Labour Income: A principal factor in the stronger income trend has been the rapid increase in labour income. Labour earnings increased 4 per cent during the 12 months between October 1960 and October 1961, and in the latest three months were 5 per cent higher.
7.	Corporate Profits:	Corporate profits,
which are particularly sensitive to changes in business conditions, have shown a rapid acceleration in 1961, and in the third quarter, were 10 per cent higher than a year earlier.
8.	Employment: The total of those with jobs rose 1.6 per cent in 1961 in comparison with 1960. In the October-December period there was an increase of more than 2 per cent, and in December alone an increase of 3 per cent. These increases have been accounted for principally by the upsurge in manufacturing, and in the latest three months manufacturing employment showed a 6 per cent increase.
9.	Unemployment: The trend in unemployment has been gradually downward since the beginning of 1961. By August, the number of unemployed persons had fallen below the level of a year earlier, and in December, was

18 per cent lower than in December a year ago. People who were unemployed in December were 115,000 fewer in number than in December a year ago.
10.	Cost of Living: It is well known that in periods of rapid economic expansion heavy upward pressure is exerted on the level of prices and hence on the cost of living. For example, between 1949 and 1961 the index of consumer prices rose by 29 per cent, or an average of 2.4 per cent per year. It is most gratifying to note, therefore, that during the first 11 months of 1961 while the government's program of national economic development was building up, the consumer price index rose by only .8 per cent or one third of the average yearly increase during the previous 12 years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to outline the steps which the government has taken to help our producers achieve the very satisfactory results I have just mentioned.
1.	We have lowered the exchange rate to a more realistic ratio with other world currencies which has had the effect of making Canadian exports more competitive in world markets, has discouraged excessive imports and has provided needed impetus to our tourist industry. The full benefits of this step should be felt increasingly during the year.
2.	We have held trade and industrial conferences in Ottawa and the provinces to bring the services of the Department of Trade and Commerce directly to businessmen in all parts of Canada. By so doing we have stimulated their interest in export trade and helped them to produce more efficiently.
3.	We have greatly expanded our trade mission and trade fair programs to show businessmen the opportunities which exist in foreign markets and help them display their products in these markets. These programs will be pushed forward and expanded during the present year. Businessmen have co-operated enthusiastically in the development of our trade mission program.
4.	We have introduced export credit facilities to provide long term financing for capital goods exports. Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak about Britain's application to enter the common market. In recent weeks few subjects have been more in the public mind than the British negotiations with the six member governments of the European economic community with a view to membership. The interest and concern of the Canadian business community regarding this important question is very natural indeed.
The Address-Mr. Hees
Early this month my cabinet colleagues and I enjoyed full and frank dicussions with Mr. Edward Heath, Lord Privy Seal of the British government, who is the minister responsible for Britain's current negotiations with the six. These useful and constructive talks were carried out in a most cordial atmosphere. Mr. Heath informed us of the current developments in the negotiations and stressed the efforts being made by Britain to safeguard the essential trade interests of Canada and other commonwealth countries.
For our part, we welcomed his statement and emphasized the extent and importance of Canadian interests in the British market. We were reassured as a result of this meeting that Great Britain has very much in mind the importance of Canadian trade interests in the United Kingdom and the need to do everything possible to safeguard those interests. We are co-operating closely with the British by providing full and complete information about Canadian interests in the British market in order that their negotiators may be in the best possible position to safeguard our trade interests.
They have asked for relevant data and this we are providing for the whole range of our exports to the United Kingdom. Today we have a group of senior and qualified officials on the spot for this purpose and to reinforce the officials who are already in Brussels and London. The officials concerned include the assistant deputy minister of trade and commerce, responsible for trade policy, and the head of the department's international trade relations branch. As the negotiations evolve we will be ensuring that the right men are in Brussels at the right time to meet the needs as they arise. Our concern is to make sure that the interests of all Canadian producers across the length and breadth of Canada are fully understood by the British. There will be, during the period of the negotiations, the closest co-operation between the British and Canadian governments.

I quote from the Financial Post of January 20, the latest issue, and this I believe is an objective newspaper which certainly has never done anything to bolster the fortunes of the Conservative party and has never been opposed, as I know it, to the Liberal party. On its front page it carries the heading:
The OUTLOOK-Weekly roundup of the latest facts and expert opinion on the economic weather ahead . . .
In this article Mr. Dalton Robertson says the following:
Three recent developments in the Canadian economy-in goods, in men, in money-reflect the burgeoning expansion of business and hold out the prospect of good times through 1962.
Canada's unemployment situation is sharply healthier than it was six months ago or a year ago.
At mid-December, seasonal factors discounted, only 6.1 per cent of the work force was unemployed. This compares with 7.4 per cent as recently as last July and a record high of 7.9 per cent a year earlier.
With the underlying trend in unemployment downward throughout 1961-in contrast to upward through 1960-it is clear that the business recovery is broadening and strengthening in the places where it counts most.
The forcefulness of the upturn in business activity shows in these bright facts:
Unemployments increase between November and December-or between September and December for that matter-is the smallest in any of the past five years. At the same time, the seasonal decline in employment between November and December is one of the smallest on record.
The 180,000 increase in employment over the past year is proportionally equal for both men and women-distinct contrast with the year-to-year increase in 1960 when almost all of the advance was in female workers getting relatively low-paid jobs.
Employment in manufacturing is up by 80,000 to 90,000 in the year-whereas in 1960, jobs in manufacturing, where the pay is highest, were on the decline.
These increases in manufacturing and, to a lesser extent, in construction employment have led to a reduction in unemployment among men. By contrast: A year ago, the increases in total employment were due to the flow of new women workers into the labour force-while slackness in manufacturing was causing lay-offs among men workers.
These trends suggest a number of good things are in store for Canada. With more family breadwinners back at the better-paying jobs, retail sales stand to make substantial gains in 1962. With a rise in total consumer spending, the whole economy will get an extra forward push.

That, Mr. Speaker, is a very objective opinion on our economy, a very thoughtful opinion indeed.
Finally, I would like to speak about the economic outlook for the year we are just beginning. The Canadian economy is entering a new period of sound expansion and in my recent travels across the country I have found that our producers are approaching the new year with confidence and optimism. I believe that the program of national economic development which was initiated by the government more than a year ago has made a substantial contribution to our fortunes. However, it is our businessmen, our industrial workers, our farmers, our fishermen, our lumbermen, our miners, and other primary producers with their enterprise, ingenuity and skill who have made our economy move steadily forward. They have our gratitude and admiration and we look forward to working with them in the year ahead, as we have worked together in the year that has just ended.
If we can achieve that essential co-operation between management and labour, which is so necessary to make our products competitive in an increasingly competitive world, there are no heights of economic progress which we cannot reach. With government, labour and management working together as a team we can, and I believe we will, make 1962 the most prosperous year this country has ever known.

Any group of salesmen can easily sell products with exaggerated promises of high performance, but the second or third time around, they will find the going a little rough. So, too, with the members on the treasury benches opposite. As salesmen they are finding the going tougher and tougher because the results that they have given to the Canadian people have been so poor.
In Windsor, Nova Scotia, the Minister of Public Works had this to say:
The Liberals were in power for 22 years and it seems that a strong Liberal bias has been built up in most of the press, and broadcasting, as you must all realize daily.

We have come to a new year and the government is now embarking upon a set of new proposals to help us cure our ills. Before giving consideration to these proposals as contained in the speech from the throne I thought it might be well to go back to 1961 in retrospect because events and measures that were taken in that year were harbingers of things to come in this year.
