According to the press, the Prime Minister said in Ottawa on December 20:
It has been a wonderful year for me. I look back on the year with a good deal of pleasure, both personally and politically.
I am glad the Prime Minister had a wonderful year personally, but I think that many people in Canada and many of his followers would be much more satisfied if he had had a better year politically.
The year 1961 began and ended on a rather comic opera note, with a great deal of tragedy thrown in between for the Canadian people. I have tabulated month by month a few items of political significance that caused dismay and suffering among our people. They also caused a loss of prestige to our government both at home and abroad. In January, for instance, the Prime Minister went down to Washington to sign the Columbia river treaty during the dying days of the Eisenhower administration. He did not at that time have a signed agreement with the government of British Columbia, the government most vitally interested. In a similar situation, when the St. Lawrence seaway project was developed, Ontario and the state of New York joined to develop this power and before signing any international agreement with the United States Mr. St. Laurent had an agreement signed with the province of Ontario.
The failure of the government to do this has brought about all kinds of complicated negotiations between them and the government of British Columbia. These negotiations have had a comic aspect although they should be of grave concern to all Canadians and especially the people of British Columbia.
We have had the spectacle of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the premier of British Columbia playing hide and seek with one another in Vancouver and Victoria. Also, the Minister of Justice, in a speech in his native province of British Columbia, denounced Premier Bennett and caused an international incident by denouncing Mr. Udall, secretary of the interior of the United States, at the same time.
On another occasion, to assure us that there was some harmony at least between the two governments and that they were not completely on a war footing, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) came into this house and said that the premier of British Columbia had gretted him with the words, "Hello, Columbia". The Columbia river is carried forward as unfinished business into 1962.
February of last year has a record for that month. At mid-month we had 719,000 people unemployed, 12,000 more than February of the previous year. The Prime Minister and the ministers on the treasury benches did not


consider that unemployment was a problem at all in Canada until parliament was called into session the previous November. What is worse the measures taken to stimulate the economy at that time in order to increase employment were inadequate.
In March another record was established and this record was not a pleasant one for the taxpayers of Canada. In that month the Minister of Finance tabled the estimates and we learned for the first time that our budgetary spending would be over $6 billion despite the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had told the House of Commons that our expenditures would be cut by the elimination of waste and extravagance.
In April another record was set. Canadian National Railways posted the highest deficit in its history, a deficit of $67,500,000. Car-loadings have always been considered an indication of the state of our economy. Ever since this government came to power car-loadings have been down. They have been down every month compared with the corresponding month of 1956, the last year when the previous administration was in office. Not only have they been down as compared with corresponding months in the year 1956 but they are, generally, down as compared with corresponding months during worsening years of Tory rule, though there have been only one or two monthly exceptions.
In May this government put the wheels in motion to fire governor Coyne from the Bank of Canada. They did this contrary to all those high ideals of justice expressed in the immortal words of the bill of rights. I think nothing has done more harm to our prestige abroad than this particular action taken by the government at that time.
In June the Minister of Finance brought in his budget. It was a record budget with a record deficit of $650 million. I know the Minister of Finance allowed himself about $50 million leeway each way but the hon. gentleman is always modest about naming the amount of the expected deficit so I think the deficit will, in fact, be higher than this.
In July the Prime Minister talked about an election "sooner or later". He promised we should have one and issued a challenge to the Senate. Unless the Senate would withdraw its amendment to a certain bill which this house had sent to it he would go to the country over the issue of Senate reform.
In August we learned that the Minister of Finance had taken a personal interest in the unemployment insurance fund. He was taking

the hypothecated and depreciated bonds in that fund under protective wing. Now he has nothing to protect. According to the speech from the throne the taxpayers of Canada are to be allowed to make up the loss in that fund arising from mishandling and poor investment.
In this month also the people were becoming aware that we were buying United States interceptor planes. They could recall the closing down of our plant at Malton. They could recall also that at that time the completed planes were cut up into little pieces with a blow torch so as to conceal the evidence of the ingenuity, the high degree of workmanship and the productivity of Canadian workmen. The end result was a loss to Canada of valuable skilled workmen and a loss of many jobs in Canadian industry.
In September there was the Accra commonwealth conference when the government took exception to Britain joining the common market. We heard all about the published and the unpublished documents. We heard both the official and the unofficial statements made by our two ministers at that conference. After so much criticism the Minister of Finance came up with what I thought was a most novel idea. He said he was using these tactics in order to help Britain at the Brussels conference. This contention is certainly not borne out by the press in Britain. The London Times said the Canadian government was playing politics. The London Spectator said the Canadian government had no business telling Britain how to run her economy when they had made such a mess of their own.
In October the news stressed the division in the cabinet concerning the use of nuclear warheads in air defence and particularly concerning the warheads proposed to be used in the Bomarc bases. The Bomarc bases are nearing completion and some decision on this question should be reached by the government. At the present time should an occasion arise for the use of these bases we have nothing on hand as warheads except some sawdust and sand. I realize there is a difference of opinion in Canada as to whether we should have nuclear warheads or not but I think our government should take a stand. In my opinion it is irresponsible for the government to do otherwise; refusal to reach a decision is in my opinion indefensible.
In November, the dominion bureau of statistics reported that immigration was down by one third. We have since learned that during the full year 1961 more people left Canada than entered it. Many of those who left Canada were young, well trained Canadians who went elsewhere because they found 26207-1-8

They could not get jobs and they went back to their home countries. We are, in effect, exporting some of our unemployed. December is the comic opera month, because in that month we heard about the proposed firing of the Minister of Finance. We heard about the great shuffle in the cabinet that never came off. We heard about the great journey of the cabinet to Quebec. Then there was the aftermath. We heard the reference of the Prime Minister to the servile press and then there was the mutual glorification meeting in Toronto when the Prime Minister referring to the Minister of Finance said that no man could be more loyal or devoted. Our fiscal and monetary policy is basic to the welfare of all Canadians. We will have more to say about monetary policy shortly.
I have often criticised the government. At the time of the conversion loan I predicted that among its effects would be the following: it would tend to stagnate trade and cause unemployment, it would increase taxes at all levels of government for a generation, it would raise the cost of production and every new home buyer would be saddled with a mortgage at a high interest rate which he would be paying for most of his working years. I said at the same time that the government would always be a prisoner of its mistake at the time of the conversion loan. It is. It has not bothered the government that it has had to increase the gross debt by over $3 billion and our net debt by about $2 billion. They just print new money to cover the debt. But this all pales into insignificance if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) surrenders completely, and if he continues to do what he is now doing in the Department of Finance with the monetary policy. Since last June the minister has been using the printing presses to debase our currency at the rate of $5i million to $6 million a day, about three times the rate that we are plunging into debt. Debasing or watering down our dollar is something akin to a milkman watering milk. You would be fooled because the dollar and the milk would look the same afterwards but their value would be less.
I realize that where you have economic growth you must have some increase in the money supply. In the early 1950's there were four years when the money supply was increased at an average rate of $400 million a year. Now it increases that much in about as many months or three or four times faster and we have no boom such as we had to finance in those years.
The mechanics of creating new money are simple. The banks buy bonds and they can issue many times the price of those bonds in new credit. The Minister of Finance has resorted to this type of financing because he cannot get the public to buy bonds in the volume that he requires. New money is being created to buy government bonds and the public pays the interest. All economists say that it is a dangerous thing to issue a lot of new money to cover overspending, and this is exactly what we are doing at the present time. We are in a period of inflation. In 1960 even the minister himself had this to say about inflation:
Let us give no quarter to such a defeatist doctrine. Inflation acts like a drug on the economic system. Even small doses breed a craving for more.
I fear that the minister has now become an inflation addict. If the rate of inflation now


current is allowed to go on unabated, I predict dire consequences for the Canadian people. By the minister's own words, he has adopted a defeatist doctrine. The savings of citizens, whether in the banks, insurance, pensions or what not, will rapidly decrease in value if we go on this way. I say that a government that has adopted this defeatist doctrine is a menace to the welfare and future of every man, woman and child in Canada.
I read the correspondence between the minister and the new governor of the Bank of Canada and certainly the new governor does not take any responsibility in connection with the issuing of new money. That is within the responsibility of the Minister of Finance. The new governor stated that his responsibility would be the day to day operation of the bank. When the new governor presents his annual report I think he should be brought before the banking and commerce committee to tell us where we are going. My first words, Mr. Speaker, must be to congratulate the mover (Mr. Bourdages) and the seconder (Mr. Browne, Vancouver-Kingsway) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should also like to congratulate the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Flynn), the newly appointed Deputy Speaker-yourself, sir-and the parliamentary secretaries. I would be very remiss also if I did not express to the Speaker of this house what I am sure is the feeling of all of us, namely that we are glad to see him back again in good health presiding over our deliberations with fairness and, it seems to me most important of all, with unfailing good humour.
A few years ago when I first entered this house after the 1957 election, a much wiser and slightly older member of the House of Commons gave to me, as a new member, a piece of advice which I think was extremely sound. He said this: "In your parliamentary life you will find many things in which you could be vitally interested. I would suggest to you that you select three or four of those in which you are most deeply concerned and prosecute those in parliament on every logical and possible occasion. In other words do not spread yourself too thin." Following that advice, I determined that my three major projects as a member of parliament would be- to attempt to raise, if I could in some way, the economic standards of the maritime provinces of Canada; second, to concern myself with legislation concerning education, especially vocational and technical education of our youth; and third, the field of veterans legislation.
In the few minutes that I have at my disposal this afternoon I should like to talk about the first of these matters, namely our maritime economy, its problems and solutions for them.
In 1957, before the election of June 10, those of us who were selected to carry the Conservative banner in Atlantic Canada came together for a momentous meeting under four

The Address-Mr. MacRae extremely able members of our party. Those gentlemen are now the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean), the Solicitor General (Mr. Browne, St. John's West) and the hon. gentleman who is now the senator from Royal but who was formerly the minister of veterans affairs. There we drew up a platform of those things for which we would stand. Over the next few years that particular platform became known popularly as the Atlantic resolutions.
I wish to discuss these resolutions this afternoon because in that election and the next one the right hon. gentleman who is now the Prime Minister of this country promised in my constituency and in others- in fact in all of the maritime constituencies in which he appeared-that these promises would be kept. May I say that those promises have been kept in full measure. I should like to discuss each one of them in turn. The first resolution or the first plank upon which we stood in 1957 stated that there would be:
A national development program of federal assistance for developing the resources of the Atlantic provinces having regard to their different needs and varying financial capabilities.
As a tangible example of action that has been taken under this resolution, our Conservative government and those who supported it can point with pride to the roads to resources which have been built especially in our four maritime provinces. The federal government has provided over $30 million to the Atlantic provinces in this connection. It should be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that roads as such are normally a provincial responsibility. This was something that was done entirely at the expense of the federal government. These roads have opened up formerly inaccessible areas of Atlantic Canada. New airports have been built at St. John's, Gander and Halifax. Just a few days ago I was advised by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) that there was to be constructed at Fredericton a new airport building which, with its related works, will cost almost $1 million. A few years ago, one of the most contentious issues in my own province was the Beechwood power project. The federal government made a loan of $30 million at a low interest rate to New Brunswick for this vital power project. Here is something that I should like to stress, Mr. Speaker. This was a loan which had been consistently denied by the former federal Liberal government.
One of the most vital factors in the Atlantic development is the provision of cheap electrical power. This will attract industry and will put in a competitive position the products

that we are able to manufacture. This is something that was long recognized by the able gentleman who was premier of our province between the years 1952 and 1960 and who is now the genial Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming). As a result of his vision and his dynamic leadership, our province is now beginning to feel the full effects of the programs which he instituted and in which, after 1957, he was so generously aided by the Conservative government here in Ottawa.
I notice that the order paper contains a resolution in connection with a national power grid. The governments of the Hon. Hugh John Flemming and the Hon. Robert Stanfield in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia were able to show what could be done in this regard when they instituted the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia power grid just a few years ago.
Resolution No. 2 is as follows, and I quote:
Industrial decentralization; by placing a more equitable share of defence contract expenditures within the Atlantic provinces; by the establishment of crown corporations; by encouraging private enterprises to locate in the area; and by encouraging the processing here of our natural resources as a result of special fiscal considerations.
Our able Conservative government has established a small business branch within the Department of Trade and Commerce and this branch is assisting small businesses to participate more fully in defence contracts expenditures. A regional office of the Department of Trade and Commerce has been opened at Halifax and this office assists businessmen in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. A similar office has been maintained for some time in St. John's, Newfoundland. This office will place the entire resources of the Department of Trade and Commerce at the disposal of the maritime business community. We know, too, that the resources of the industrial development bank have been increased from $160 million to $400 million. Many more categories of business are eligible to borrow from this source. Double depreciation allowances are permitted businesses which locate in surplus manpower areas. This has had a very beneficial effect on some areas of the maritimes. The federal government subsidy to the shipbuilding industry is providing many more employment opportunities in the maritimes.
Now, what has been happening more specifically in New Brunswick as a province, and in my constituency in particular? Only recently an electronics plant located in Camp-bellton and it will eventually employ from 1,000 to 1,500 people, thus providing a tremendous boost to the economy of that area. I

know that the industries we have established should be based on the natural resources of our area. The greatest natural resource that we have is our forests. In Grand Falls a plant has been established which will manufacture shoe lasts; a veneer plant has been established in my constituency and a chipboard plant in Milltown, Charlotte county. There are many others.
I should like to quote from the Telegraph Journal of January 9, 1962, and in so doing I am quoting the premier of New Brunswick, a Liberal premier:
New Brunswick experiencing $100 million industrial expansion.
Projects costing $100 million and seen as likely to create at least 7,000 jobs are in definite or tentative planning stages for New Brunswick, mostly in the north and in the Saint John area.
"The future looks very bright," Liberal premier Louis J. Robichaud said in an interview. "I am confident that with co-operation of government and industry we will provide year-round jobs in New Brunswick, proportionately as many as they have in wealthier provinces."
The present Liberal administration in New Brunswick attempts to take some credit for this situation. I want to be fair and I will say they have assisted to some extent within the last year and a half. However, the great bulk of the credit for the establishment of these industries and what is happening in our province today must go to the farsighted policies of Hugh John Flemming and his Conservative government. They were aided nobly after 1957 by the farsighted policies of the Prime Minister of Canada and his able government.
Personally, in so far as public works are concerned, I would rather see a factory started in Fredericton that would give year-round employment to 200 men than all the public buildings that have been built there since confederation. I can well remember sitting in this chamber during the bitter debates after 1957 and I recall when things got too hot for the Liberals they would shout, "Twenty cents a day". Well, I should like to say that 20 cents a day is just four times the amount Mackenzie King said he would never give to any Conservative province in 1935.
You know, in Fredericton we make some of the best shoes in the world. There is the Hartt Shoe Company and the Palmer-McLel-lan Shoe Company. The first major defence contract that has come to the Palmer-McLel-lan Shoe Company in 17 years was awarded this past year, a contract for 42,000 pairs of shoes. During the past year one of the finest agricultural research stations in the whole of Canada has been built in Fredericton at a cost of about $2 million. Camp Gagetown, one of the largest and finest military camps in the
The Address-Mr. MacRae British commonwealth of nations, continues to grow. During 1957 it was said that if the Conservatives were elected this camp would be closed. However, as I have said, it has continued to grow and it is one of the finest camps in the whole of the British commonwealth.
Item No. 3 reads:
Atlantic provinces power development by means of financial assistance for the development of low-cost electric power which would fully preserve the rights of the provinces to build and operate both thermal and hydro installations and transmission lines and by immediate subvention on coal produced in the region and used for generating electric power therein.
I have mentioned the Beechwood power development and the power grids that were established. The government, in a tangible way, provided loans for 40 years at a low rate of interest for the establishment of the power grid between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Mr. Arthur Johnson, the past president of the Atlantic economic council-a most worthy organization-has said that this grid has saved the two provinces the incredible sum of $60 million annually.
In the past four years, coal assistance in the form of subventions has been more than doubled. To be specific, in 1956-57 federal payments for coal subventions were just under $7 million and in 1960-61 they amounted to over $15 million.
Item No. 4 reads:
Adjustment of freight rates and provision of transportation facilities to allow our producers reasonable access to the markets of Canada.
Transportation is one of the keys to our whole economic well-being in Atlantic Canada. We know, of course, that the federal government pays subventions on freight rates every year amounting to about $14 million. All of us have been anticipating with deep interest the second volume of the report of the royal commission on transportation which was tabled today. I have not had an opportunity of reading it but it is my hope, and the hope of all of us, that it will contain many recommendations which will go some distance toward solving this difficult problem. We need a national policy on transportation. We do not accept the recommendation of the Gordon commission that we leave the mari-times, nor are we going to be second-class citizens in that part of Canada. I have every faith that the McPherson report will suggest some solution which will correct the injustice under which the maritime provinces now suffer.
Item No. 5 reads:
Capital projects program to provide federal capital assistance for provincial projects designed to enlarge the basic economy of the area.

The Address

Mr. MacRae
I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that in my discussion of the first item, a national development program, I have shown that this plan has been implemented in good measure. There are other projects about which we feel rather strongly, some more strongly than others, and for which I would urge continuing government consideration. There is the causeway to Prince Edward Island and the corridor road through Maine as well as the integrated development of Saint John river power. I would urge the power development of the huge Passama-quoddy project, and I should like to mention the Chignecto canal project. I was disappointed last fall when it was shown that, as a transportation project, the Chignecto was not feasible. I was delighted, however, when the Prime Minister said the government of Canada would take another look at this project to see whether, from a power angle, it would be feasible. I hope something will be worked out as a result of that.
Another item or promise in 1957 was the establishment of the Canadian coast guard. This was of vital importance to our fishermen and others who follow the sea. This has been done as promised.
Finally, in 1957 there was the special adjustment grant for all provinces with a per capita income substantially below the national average. In 1958 the government undertook to provide an additional $100 million in the Atlantic provinces grants over a four year period; effective in 1962 this grant will be raised.
There has been considerable discussion this past year in my native province about federal contributions to New Brunswick and a completely unfounded statement that contributions have decreased. A political football was made of this in the past year but the true facts are that in 1956 the total of unconditional and conditional grants and payments to New Brunswick was $29.5 million and in 1961-62 these grants will amount to $60.5 million, or more than double.
What about social justice payments? In the year 1956-57 the Liberal administration made payments in New Brunswick of approximately $46 million. In 1960-61 that figure had increased by almost 60 per cent to $75.5 million. Figures do not lie, Mr. Speaker. They are there on the record.
When Liberal party spokesmen talk of discrimination against New Brunswick, as they have done in the past year and a half, let us remember that the per capita amount received by New Brunswick from tax rental in 1956-57, when the Liberal party was in


office, was $32.11 per person. In 1961-62 it amounts, with the addition of Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, to $56.24 per person, and in 1962-63 it will amount to $58.12. It is worthy of note that the national average is $48.64 per capita, and therefore I do not feel we have any complaint there.
I have discussed the part that the federal Conservative government is playing in the resurgence of our maritime provinces at present, but even though they are the most important member of the team bringing this about, we must never forget there are other players on the team as well. The provincial governments must carry their share of the load. Far too often our provincial governments have wasted their energy and their efforts in petty jealousy and quarrels. Also, the management of our industries must be willing not only to co-operate but give their full support. They must remember that the well-being of those who work for them will reflect in their prosperity.
Finally, labour must use common sense. Far too often the working man has been misled by unscrupulous labour leaders. I do not say that is so true of Canada, but we have only to look at the Hoffas and Becks in the United States to see what I mean. Labour must be made to realize that we cannot price ourselves out of our own and foreign markets by demanding more for our labour, services and products than others can or will pay.
We in the maritimes, and as a matter of fact Canadians in all parts of the country, will have to realize that there is nothing free. A year and a half ago, in June, 1960, the majority of the people of New Brunswick temporarily accepted the premise that they could receive free hospitalization, and in so believing they turned out the most able premier and government that they had had for decades.
There is a cartoonist whose work I admire greatly, Collins of the Gazette. He draws that familiar figure of the little man in the barrel, with the derby hat and bristling mustache, usually labelled "You know who". A few months ago he drew a cartoon and, the saying has it that a picture is worth more than a thousand words. It seemed to me this cartoon was worth even more than that. It shows our little man in a supermarket, having the most wonderful time in the world filling up his shopper's cart with all the packages that are marked "free". There is free government this and free government that, and he goes along until his cart becomes so piled up that he can hardly see over it. Then the final drawing shows him reaching the cash register, with a long cash register tape and a woebegone

look. The caption underneath says "You have to reach the check-out counter sometime". We all have to reach the check-out counter sometime in our spending as well as everything else.
There is a new spirit in Atlantic Canada today, a resurgence of pride and a spirit of well being that was not there before 1957. For a century it was said that the maritimes greatest export was brains, but today educated men and women are staying in the maritime provinces, as well as those who have not the advantage of the education they might like to have, because there is more opportunity there than ever before. I feel, too, that under this government and its dynamic policy of national development in all areas of Canada, our part of this great nation will continue to grow and prosper as it rightly should.

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all join with those who have congratulated the mover (Mr. Bourdages) and the seconder (Mr. Browne, Vancouver-Kings-way) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As for you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, whom I had the privilege of knowing for a long time as a painstaking and hard worker, I am convinced that you will carry out efficiently the new duties entrusted to you. You have been elected by the house with an overwhelming majority to replace the member called to the cabinet. You will only have to study the work accomplished by the Speaker of this house and to follow the example set by him since his appointment to this high office in 1957, and I am sure that you will find only friends on both sides of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to touch upon every subject mentioned in the speech from the throne nor do I propose to point out the numerous omissions which characterize that speech more than its contents.
The leader of the Liberal party, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has done that tremendously well in his speech yesterday, and I believe a certain number of my colleagues will take up a few points in particular. That is why I will limit myself today to one point only, that is the amendments to the constitution.
I must say first of all that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) made an honest effort in his suggestions to the provinces. He would have been the first one to admit, I am sure, that his proposals could not all be accepted and that they would even be the subject of lengthy discussions. Indeed, I could not understand how a sensible man would expect his first proposals to be accepted immediately since it is most dangerous to amend the constitution.
We will soon be celebrating the centennial of confederation. We should not pass premature amendments, amendments where caution would be thrown to the winds and which would only make it worse for Canada. And besides, if you read what Father Ares, Jesuit, has written about these amendments, you can see that nowadays you cannot be too cautious before touching them.
It is best to wait in order to make sure that mutual understanding will persist, complete mutual understanding in all fields of endeavour of the Canadian people, in order to build up mutual confidence and mutual respect throughout Canada, before tackling the ticklish matter of amending the constitution.

The Address-Mr. Caron
It would be best to wait a year or two, even three, before bringing our constitution back home.
It has been in England now for nearly a century, and we have always managed to survive and even to improve our lot, despite what is being said in some circles.
That is why I am asking the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) not to speed things up. I am asking his leader, the Prime Minister, not to be too much in a hurry to link his name to the repatriation of the constitution. When the constitution does come back, it should be such that we should not have to blame ourselves for acting too hastily.
Speaking of the repatriation of the constitution brings to mind an exceedingly delicate matter, a topic on which many words and much breath have been wasted. I refer to separatism, a movement which sprang up some time ago in the province of Quebec.
Of course, as opposed to some Quebec Conservative members, I have no connection with that movement, quite the contrary, and the fact is rather well known.
Is that movement really serious? I do not think it is, not for the moment at least. You only have scattered efforts by various groups without a leader in the true sense of the word. If they had men like Hitler, Mussolini, Bourguiba, Castro or even Camilien Houde, great demagogues, we might have reasons to fear an early split within confederation. As it is, the movement is already divided among capitalists, socialists, to mention only those two. No wonder, because with our Latin temperament, it is extremely difficult for us to work together. We are so individualistic.
Would it be beneficial to turn the province of Quebec into a French Canadian republic? I would be inclined to answer yes, in certain respects. It would certainly promote the development of French culture completely freed from English influence which taints our language with anglicisms. But the separatist movement, which is not new, will have the great advantage of awakening English speaking Canadians and prompt them to a careful self-examination. For, let us not forget that if there is a separatist movement in Quebec, the majority group is chiefly responsible for its existence.
In 1867, when confederation was born, we were in theory equal partners. But unfortunately things were different in practice. What fuss, what inconsistencies, had to be put up with. The provinces with English speaking majorities saw as one of the greatest advantages of confederation a means of anglicizing more easily the French Canadian nation.

Immediately after confederation, have we not seen the New Brunswick government forbid the teaching of French and religion in the schools, ostensibly because that teaching was only tolerated before confederation. It had, nevertheless, been specified under the Confederation Act that any legislation prior to confederation should be maintained. But so-called tolerance then disappeared. Fortunately, the situation has since improved.
When Manitoba entered into confederation, towards 1870-the union was completed in 1871-Sir Georges-Etienne Cartier, recalling what had happened in New Brunswick, was cautious enough to include clause 22 to protect the minority of that province.
Despite the laws, around 1890 the English speaking majority in Manitoba managed to persecute the French speaking minority and their schools. The law had been disregarded. Slowly things got better.
In 1911, it was the turn of Ontario, when that province passed the notorious regulation 17 outlawing French schools.
Then it was Saskatchewan, around 1928, under the leadership of Mr. Anderson, and bitter criticism against the Gardiner government because it tolerated religious habits and the crucifix in Catholic schools. He knew how to excite the passions of the Anglo-Canadian majority in that province and overthrew the Gardiner government to set up his own persecuting laws.
Even British Columbia, to a lesser degree, however, proved extremely narrow-minded.
But let us rejoice, persecutions began on the Atlantic coast and reached British Columbia; let's hope they have been drowned in the Pacific.
Outside the province of Quebec, French Canadians have been treated as poor relatives, even within the federal service. How many senior positions have we held in the civil service? Did we not have the necessary qualifications? That was not the reason because in proportion to the number, we were just as qualified, if not more. Most of our candidates to senior positions had the advantage of being bilingual.
Such an attitude was equivalent to giving French Canadians a certificate of incompetence that they did not deserve.
During the last session, I recommended during the debate on the Civil Service Act that an additional 5 per cent be paid to anyone who could prove that he was bilingual, not only for new positions but also for promotions. There was practically no discussion on that issue; there was no serious examination and the majority in the house,

except for two or three Conservative members voted for refusing that right to intellectual superiority. I am happy to see that the Liberals and the C.C.F. have unanimously supported my motion.
What is one to think of that decision of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) who, in his proposed building program for the next few years (about 15 projects) and in spite of the advantage found in the fact that Hull is close to the centre block of parliament did not give any thought about locating a single building on the Quebec side, in Hull or vicinity.
A short while ago, the Post Office Department requested the appointment of a superintendent for district No. 2. This district covers the ridings of Pontiac, Gatineau, Hull, Papineau, Argenteuil, part of Labelle, Glen-garry-Prescott, Russell, Ottawa East, Ottawa West, part of Carleton, Stormont and a few others where the French speaking population is at least equal to the English speaking population if not in majority. I asked that the civil service commission be urged to select a bilingual candidate for that position. At that time the Postmaster General replied that the decision was up to the civil service commission, which is not entirely true because the civil service commission accepts the qualifications required by the department. Generally, it is the deputy minister who makes a decision (sometimes after consultation, sometimes on his own). The civil service commission could not require a bilingual candidate for that position because the department made no such request.
And what about the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) who did not appoint a single French Canadian to any important position? It could be that the minister did not try too hard.
Were we too shy to claim vigorously what belonged to us by rights? We have perhaps a certain responsibility in that regard, but could the majority not be a little more generous? Could the English Canadian majority not behave like true Anglo-Saxons? Before the situation deteriorates, as Great Britain did for several of its colonies to which it granted independence before it was too late to keep them as friends and customers, could the majority not prevent such difficulties?
What meanness was shown when the French Canadians started asking for a distinctive national flag, without any symbol of interdependence. There were cries of indignation from various English sections of Canada, from the Daughters of the British Empire, the Veterans Association, the Orange
The Address-Mr. Caron Sentinel and many more. We even heard Mr. Smallwood, after having supported the entry of Newfoundland into confederation, say that as far as he was concerned, there would be only one flag, the union jack.
He became a Canadian, but his soul still belongs to England, because the union jack is a combination of three crosses: St. Andrew's cross, St. Patrick's cross and St. George's cross, representing the three countries which joined together to form the United Kingdom: Scotland, Ireland and England.
As for the Veterans Association, do those who live outside of Quebec not remember that, during the 1914 and 1939 wars, the heroic deeds of our troops could seem to be those of English soldiers, since there was only the union jack?
Talking about the veterans, on November 11, 1961, a remembrance ceremony had been organized at Lansdowne park before the football game. In the parade could be seen six or seven union jacks, one American flag and only one Canadian flag, the Red Ensign. The band played only "God save the Queen" and did not bother at all with "O Canada". Is this not ridiculous? Everyone claims to be a Canadian but such actions show the contrary.
How about the constant opposition to the request for bilingual cheques made year after year. Was it really necessary to introduce motions to request bilingual cheques when, according to the B.N.A. Act, all official documents of the federal government can be bilingual. My cheque is an official document. It was just as easy to make it bilingual as it was for Mr. Veniot to introduce bilingual stamps in the Post Office Department. It would have been as easy to introduce bilingual cheques as it was for the Liberal party to repair the sorry situation of two currencies one English and the other French, when they introduced bilingual currency.
One Mr. Jacques Gagnon, of 127 Ste. Marie street in Hull, told me about his experience with the federal police patrolling the parkways. Referring to the famous expression "I don't speak French" here is what he says:
Besides, that does not surprise me any more. Again, I had received that answer from an officer of the Royal Mounted Police, on December 12 last, when I was arrested on the Gatineau Parkway, not far from Gamelin boulevard. I had been ordered to check with Ottawa, on Wellington street, where nobody spoke my language, absolutely no one out of 15 police officers who were in that office.
Now, don't tell me that the federal police is so totally deprived of bilingual employees that a French Canadian who does not speak English has to go around with a pocket
110	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Caron dictionary in order to make himself understood by the federal mounted police in Ottawa.
I am not blaming the policeman on duty, but the officers who are so ill-advised as to place him in such a false position.
Another thing which has often displeased visitors to the parliament buildings is the fact that, with certain members of the House of Commons police, it was almost impossible to make themselves understood if they spoke French. It would have been so easy to show the real character of the federal government in requiring that all those employees be bilingual. All French Canadians are bilingual; some English Canadians are, but they are not the majority.
The same applies to the R.C.M.P. on duty around the parliament buildings. The odd officer speaks French, but the great majority do not understand a single word of French. When I brought up the matter, I was told that efforts were being made to place, as much as possible, bilingual officers on duty on parliament hill. I can assure you that the efforts were not very successful.
There should also be on duty, at any time of the day, a bilingual official at each Canadian port, but it is not so.
In our diplomatic corps also, there should not be a single unilingual diplomat because a country is often characterized abroad by its diplomats. It should not be more difficult for an English speaking Canadian, especially for a scholar, to learn French than it is for a French Canadian to learn English.
I remember once going to Paris as a delegate to attend a meeting of NATO parliamentarians and what surprised me most was the fact that the delegates from all other countries were bilingual or trilingual, including those from England. The only unilingual delegates were the English Canadian and American delegates.
I know that in some places I will be accused of fanaticism. Am I a fanatic when I ask that the French and Catholic minority groups be treated at least according to the spirit if not the letter of the law?
Am I a fanatic when I ask that French Canadians in the provinces with an English majority be given the same treatment as the English minority in the province of Quebec as far as schools are concerned.
Am I a fanatic when I claim for my compatriots a chance to accede to the higher positions in the civil service of my country?
Am I a fanatic when I ask that my fellow French Canadians be served in French in the custom ports of this country?


Am I a fanatic when I insist that our representatives abroad be in a position to show a true picture of Canada where two races and two cultures live side by side? And I could go on forever quoting examples but this would not add strength to my argument.
I do not care, Mr. Speaker, if English speaking or French speaking Canadians learn English or French. What I want is recognition of the superiority of those who took the trouble to learn both languages and I want them to obtain preference from the civil service commission. This would be an incentive to others.
I hope that the majority which is directly responsible for this separatist outburst in the province of Quebec will make a serious selfexamination and act, for once, like true Anglo-Saxons. The majority would then realize that French Canadians have shown themselves truly anxious to comply with all the provisions of the Confederation Act.
Quebec has never treated the English minority of that province like a poor relative. Why should the other provinces not follow that example, so that after a hundred years in the confederative pact, it could be truly said that we have really become equal partners.
All those grievances do not mean that I am in favour of separatism; I feel that that movement is too risky and has too many disadvantages for the province of Quebec and for French Canadians in the other provinces.
If such a movement were to succeed, what would be the lot of French Canadian minorities in the other provinces except in New Brunswick where the minority represents about 47 per cent of the population. Left to themselves, those minorities would be easy prey for those who would anglicize us, and our fine French culture would be limited to the province of Quebec; Canada would thus become poorer not wealthier.
Considering the plight of our brothers who live in other provinces, I feel that separatism is an attitude of unspeakable selfishness towards more than a million of our compatriots.
It will be objected that the sacrifices we have to make to maintain a mixed culture impair the quality of spoken French because numerous English expressions continuously find their way into our conversation. I ask the question: Is that really true?
We know that all modem languages have developed from the corruption of two or more foreign languages. French is a smooth blend of Latin, Greek and Frankish. Many words were added to the English language by the Normans. You will note that all words ended

in "al" and "ion" are French words. The same holds true in respect of Spanish and Portuguese. Is it really so bad that the French language in Canada, by adding certain English words to its wealth, be somewhat different from the French language spoken nowadays in France?
How many words and phrases did we not retain here, in this country, old French words and phrases which have completely disappeared from the stock of words used in France. For goodness' sake, let us not make a tragedy of the fact that our French is in a constant state of flux. Even in the various parts of France, there are great differences, and no one thinks it is a crime. For goodness' sake, just as no one should be a better Catholic than the Pope, so we should not be more French than the French themselves.
Another danger may come up in the economic field. Is it believable that a country with a population of five, six, or seven million people could successfully compete on the world markets? We find that the European countries have formed the common market and the free trade area to compensate for the deficiencies of a too small population. Could the province of Quebec do better than those countries? No.
Moreover, the separation of Quebec would mean almost insuperable difficulties for the maritime provinces if they did not get outside assistance from the United Kingdom or the United States. What would be the position of Ontario, which would have to support the west alone, and more particularly the prairie provinces in their lean years. The difficulties would be almost insuperable. The resulting upset would make the whole of Canada powerless with regard to its domestic problems and insignificant on the international level.
We can always improve our economic position and, in this respect, must commend the premier of the province of Quebec for finding out that all our eggs unfortunately seemed to be put in one basket. He therefore went to Italy and France trying to find new investment capital in order to diversify existing industries and create new ones in Quebec. In so doing, he served not only the province of Quebec but the whole of Canada.
The separatist movement has no chance of succeeding at this time. But I warn English Canadians to hurry and revert to the spirit of confederation, which aimed at the integration-not the assimilation-of French Canadians. If not, though you may celebrate the centenary of that memorable pact, your efforts to appease the separatist feeling will not succeed, and it will only need an able leader to upset everything. Nothing but the
The Address-Mr. Pigeon good faith of the majority, which has everything to gain by showing some magnanimity, can save confederation.
The English speaking provinces should consider the Quebec school laws and rectify the discrimination against minorities in other provinces, where they are overtaxed for the maintenance of their schools, whereas, in Quebec, the minority looks after its own business.
In spite of all our difficulties and all the deficiencies we may find among our English fellow citizens, we have to admit that things are constantly improving for us, even though this improvement is very slow.
Let us always keep in mind that a people which does not want to die always asserts itself in the end.
Let us be French Canadians, fundamentally attached to our language and customs, but let us also be Canadians for the greater benefit of our country as a whole.
Let us see, for instance, what has happened in Switzerland over the last 600 years. That country is made up of Germans, French and Italians, and its leaders have succeeded in having the three languages taught in the schools and in creating a nation that is truly Swiss. It is different from all other nations and it has its own characteristics that are recognized throughout the world. It has made up a people that gets along almost anywhere. In fact, I have met Swiss people recently who have made their homes in Ontario and in Quebec. It is thanks to that triple culture that they were able to find a place for themselves almost anywhere in Canada.

The selection of the member for St. Hy-acinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), to fill the post of

The Address-Mr. Pigeon parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, was a most happy one. His work and attendance record in the house have set him up as an example.
We all rejoice, I am sure, at the good tidings which Her Majesty the Queen's worthy representative brought us in the speech from the throne. All the provinces rightly rejoice over the measures announced by the government. As for Quebec, the people realize that the present government will soon give them a railroad in the Gaspe peninsula which will develop an important area too long neglected by the former Liberal administration. The Gaspe Copper Mines were waiting for that news to invest several additional millions of dollars in the district which will soon be the scene of an extraordinary economic growth.
Recently, I was reading in a magazine all the economic advantages which will result from the construction of that railroad.
The people of that district have long been requesting the construction of a railroad on the north side of the Gaspe peninsula. As far back in 1881, La Minerve, a newspaper which was most popular in its days, published an article to the effect that the construction of a railroad was essential to the economic development of the Gaspe peninsula.
Since this railroad will bring its products to the market, the Federal Metal Company, a metal refining plant at Ste. Anne des Monts, will be able to start producing from 800 to 1,000 tons daily.
Gaspe Copper Mines, of Murdochville, will cut down its shipping costs by sending its ore to Ste. Anne des Monts instead of Gaspe. The distance is the same-69 miles-but the incline will be in favour of Ste. Anne.
Two important saw mills, those of James Richardson, at Cap Chat, and of J. A. Couturier, at Marsoui, will be able to undertake the production of wood chips, a material which cannot be shipped otherwise than by rail and which has an extremely good rating on the market.
Farmers who own wood lots will be in a position to sell their non-marketable timber for the production of chips.
The Ungava Transport Company was only waiting for that link before building and putting into operation between the north and south shores a ferry boat capable of carrying trucks and vans. The steamship La Gaspe-sienne which operates at present between Ste. Anne des Monts and Sept lies, is not readily apt for that kind of transportation.


These, Mr. Speaker, are briefly, some of the economic advantages which will be brought about by the construction of a railroad in that area.
I should be remiss if I did not point out the hard work of the hon. member for that riding, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. English) who, with the co-operation of his colleagues from Quebec, worked without rest to obtain the construction of that railroad which is essential not only to the economy of the Gaspe peninsula but also to the general economy of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that the elimination of tolls on certain bridges of the Montreal district, by arrangement with all parties concerned, will help develop business, industry and tourism on the south shore.
The announcement some time ago by the right hon. Prime Minister that the border waters commission was considering the Richelieu waterway indicates that this government intends to give the province of Quebec legislation which was indiscriminately withheld by the former minister of transport, who is today the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to quote from an article published at the time in Le Devoir of Montreal, that is on Thursday, May 20, 1954. Here is what Mr. Vigeant wrote:
Anti-Quebec speech by Mr. Chevrier.
In connection with the impending retirement of the Minister of Transport, Mr. Lionel Chevrier, and of the Minister of Finance, Mr. Douglas Abbott, we put forward the opinion, a few days ago, that we could hardly expect our interests to be defended by English speaking Quebec ministers or by French speaking Ontario ministers. After Mr. Abbott, Mr. Lionel Chevrier has just undertaken to show the soundness of our argument.

While defending the bill providing for the setting up of a railway between Beattyville-Chibougamau and St. Felicien, he delivered a speech against Quebec. Not only did he turn down the claims voiced by the members of the Saguenay district and the members who supported them.
"Adding insult to injury", as he would say, he strongly admonished them and sermonized Quebecers who dare to claim their autonomy or complain that they are not getting their share from the federal government.
And Mr. Pierre Vigeant goes on to say:
Mr. Chevrier was quite energetic in his reply. He accused Mr. Gagnon of working against national unity and he added that his arguments were both false and insignificant. Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make those remarks before coming to the heart of the matter.
There have always been numerous reasons for French Canadian dissatisfaction with the federal government. Some were well-founded and others were merely based on prejudice. However, one of the most serious causes of discontent of French Canadians throughout Canada, and not only in Quebec, was undoubtedly the offhand and indifferent attitude of the previous government not only towards the French Canadian minority, but towards all minorities in Canada. And minorities then included everything that was not Liberal, not Grit.

Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I seriously think that the previous government which could have done so much during the 22 years it was in power, is greatly responsible for the discontent of certain groups of Canadians. Some people were driven to despair by the lack of understanding of the government of the time.
Need I illustrate the point? In 1942, there was only one member from Quebec in the Canadian cabinet.
Mr. Speaker, after 90 years of confederation, it has been found that contacts and lines of communications have been established from north to south and from south to north. It has also been realized that two great racial groups could live side by side indefinitely, respect and help one another, with no love lost between them. Love is a feeling which cannot be imposed; either you love or you do not love. But I will not have anybody ever questioning the French Canadian's dedication, nor his patriotism. It seems to me that the contributions of French Canadians to public affairs, the co-operation they have given the authorities, their graves which are scattered
The Address-Mr. Pigeon all over the military cemeteries of Europe and Asia, are sufficient proof of the patriotism and sacrifices of my fellow French Canadians.
Despite the best intentions in the world, no matter how perfect the judicial and constitutional framework, it may be that the 1867 confederation is no longer suited to the needs of 1962. Perhaps we, the representatives and mandatories of the whole Canadian nation, should examine our conscience and ask ourselves if we have really discharged all our public and official duties.
Let us ask ourselves whether major amendments should not be brought to confederation, or whether it should not be reconsidered in the light of present circumstances and of rightful aspirations of the various ethnic groups which constitute the Canadian nation. And once we have noted the shortcomings and virtues of our present constitutional system, perhaps there will no longer be any reason to talk about secession but simply of complete and genuine Canadianism.
In a few years, Mr. Speaker, our great country will be a hundred years old. Already, in many places, people think of the most adequate and noble way to celebrate that century of Canadian existence. Does it not seem, Mr. Speaker, that the best approach, in such circumstances, would be to give birth to a true Canadian way of life, commensurate with our history and our responsibilities.
An event of such significance occurs but once in a man's life and it is not without great emotion that we Canadians will witness the first centennial of the country where it is most agreeable to live in these troubled times. We are the privileged children of an improved civilization, entirely devoted to the service of man. The symbol of the evolution this country is undergoing is found in this house itself where, today, members can express themselves freely in their own language, knowing in advance that they will be heard and understood by their colleagues of another origin.

It has taken 90 years to come to the system of simultaneous interpretation, first because science at that time did not make it possible for us to dream of such a complicated device and also because statesmen did not keep pace with scientific progress.
National unity is the end product of moral and spiritual components which are found in the chairs of our universities, in our trade unions, in our armed forces, in the Sunday sermon and, above all, in the heart of each
114	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Pigeon of us. We have inherited a long and glorious tradition after hard and often needless fights. Not that our forbears were mistaken about the value of the things they fought for, but actually because the mental attitude of some of their contemporaries made these fights possible although they were not necessary.
This national unity so often praised on the hustings and in this house is our own heritage for which we are in some way responsible. Perhaps not the members of this parliament personally but the members of parliament for the whole of Canada who, since 1840 and after 1867, have edified the structure of the great Canadian way of life which has fostered the development of our nation.
The great interplay of historic circumstances made possible the blending of Canadian sentiments and the communion of our minds and hearts in the pursuits of a common ideal. However, we have no right to delude ourselves nor to let our imagination summon empty dreams. This national unity, which we welcome, must be pursued from day to day and is each and everyone's business.
I even wonder whether the expression "national unity" has not been made out-ofdate by events and whether we should not rather say "national awareness". Indeed, "national unity" has been for a long time a fact in our schools, at our public meetings, in our churches, before being confirmed and sealed on the battlefields all over the world.
The problem we are facing now is one of strengthening within the Canadian state this spirit of national unity based on centuries of tradition and fashioned in the Canadian mind by British institutions adapted to North American conditions in the 19th and 20th centuries. This awareness may be found in the numerous aspects of our literature, of our newspapers, of our radio and television which, most of the time, present the true image of our life in Canada, the life which is familiar to Canadians. Nevertheless, we still lack a most important symbol of our "national awareness", a symbol around which school children gather to sing the national anthem in the morning, and which is the rallying point of our soldiers on the battlefield or the last sight of the sinking ship. That symbol, as you have recognized it, is the flag. And we still have no flag. Or rather, we have too many flags, but not a single one which would identify our soldiers abroad or our athletes taking part in international competitions. A flag is not only the symbol of an adult nation: it is also the result of that nationality itself, its official confirmation by way of enactment from the responsible authorities. Is there anything 

more depressing for the Canadian delegates to international conferences than to realize the importance of having one's own flag?
We not only need a flag; we also need a national anthem. Is it not disappointing for our official representatives, when they visit other countries, not to find the spot of native land that a flag and a national anthem would symbolize? Canada is an adult nation. Our men and our women have left their marks in many fields. We have achieved the stature of a major country, but there is nothing to prove it to the face of the world. Until the Canadian government has discharged the sacred responsibility, as bestowed upon it by its terms of reference, of selecting a national flag and a national anthem, we will always look like poor relatives in a world searching for true friends. The time has come for this house to assume before history the great responsibility of deciding what will be our national flag and what will be our national anthem. As things are going now, our country will be one hundred years old and we shall have no flag to hoist on the 1st of July, 1967, and our young Canadians will have nothing to sing on this memorable day which will mark our first centenary. It is our duty to assume our responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, I have introduced a motion in this house asking for the setting up of a committee of both houses before which official organizations representing the authorities would express their views so that our hope of having a national flag may be fulfilled. I would be very glad if this motion were agreed to. We could then invite the premiers of the ten provinces to appear before this committee and know what are the views of Messrs. Smallwood and Bennett concerning a distinctive Canadian flag.
Mr. Speaker, it is commonplace in the foreign countries to point out the good feelings between the main ethnical groups in our country. Would it not be possible to transpose this wonderful lesson of national co-operation on a higher level, thus inspiring the concert of nations.
Even at the time of the league of nations, our delegates were showing poise and selfassurance. It is a known fact that Canada has no territoral ambitions, that it does conceal any covetousness, and that, having realized at home harmony and co-operation, it can share its recipes for friendship and co-operation with the other countries of the world.
It is probably not by mere chance that the original form of the British commonwealth of nations should have been developed by a Canadian. It was quite understandable that one of our most brilliant statesmen at the time should bring into the solution of our relations

with other countries of the British empire the same pattern followed in the Canadian parliament in the light of our tradition. This British family of nations, which progressively emerged in the world between 1896 and 1931, including the glorious and decisive periods of 1919 and 1927, introduced into international law a formula both revolutionary and simple which was confirmed by the treaty of Westminster, on December 11, 1931. British statesmen-and in this regard some of our great Canadian parliamentarians are in no way inferior to them-have always kept pace with developments. The commonwealth was no more a laboratory product or an artificial creation in 1931 than the new commonwealth is now after weathering the Suez crisis in 1956. I believe together with many of my colleagues, that when the interest of the nation is at stake, there should be no party barriers. Besides, we in this house should all have enough patriotism and common sense to forget the strict discipline of political parties to join with the leader in whom the Canadian people has put its confidence in order to support him wholeheartedly and assure him of our most enlightened co-operation.
Mr. Speaker, the student of politics knows that British politics, and therefore Canadian politics until 1931, have always consisted in adapting formulas to facts while giving principles the best possible direction. When the Canadian parliament got its sovereignty, it had inherited that way of thinking and the ways of Cromwell, Curzon and Lloyd George had set a fashion here. It is therefore in no way surprising that the same flexible and fearless attitude which made it possible for this country to remain faithful to the throne while unobtrusively establishing a separation could be found in men like Lafontaine and Baldwin, Macdonald and Cartier, Borden and Diefenbaker. It was a Conservative government who appointed our first diplomatic agent in London. It was also a Conservative government who established Canadian troops as a distinctive unit in the first world war. It was the Hon. Mr. Borden who valiantly fought to have Canada sign the treaty of Versailles on its own behalf, and not as a junior partner nor in the shadow of the British flag, but as the first overseas country freely linked to its British sovereign. It also was a Conservative government which succeeded in obtaining the statute of Westminster.
It was under a Conservative government that simultaneous translation of debates was introduced in this house, as well as in the parliamentary committees. Furthermore, it is now the task of a Conservative government to reaffirm before the world the dignified and special position of this country in the world, in the economic field.
The Address-Mr. Pigeon
We belonged to the league of nations, we now belong to the United Nations. We are a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, we contribute to the Colombo plan and we have saved the new commonwealth formula in 1956. Is there another country in the world which can boast of so many positive actions in favour of world peace? Is there, even within the commonwealth, another country which has contributed more to international stability and to the rational economy which we need so much. There remains for us to make an historical and rational gesture, and I have no doubt that once again it will be made by a Conservative government. I refer to our full participation in the inter-American system, which we can achieve by becoming a full member of the organization of American states. It would seem that, in this respect, our predecessors had unjustified and no doubt unjustifiable fears.
This means that, not only are we not split between two poles, but that, on the contrary, we are the link between two great systems, two great schools of thought and, especially, two great historical realities: Europe, with its heritage of nobility and greatness; America, with its wealth and its future.
In such circumstances, it is therefore imperative that Canada, while maintaining its links with the British commonwealth of nations, for as long a time as its interests will require, should not however neglect its obligations towards the American continent. Now, there already exists that marvelous organization of American states, which superseded in 1948 the pan-American union, and which includes all countries of the American continent except Canada. Evolving from the prophetic dream of Simon Bolivar in 1826, the organization is today the finest expression of the yearning of those who wish to live in peace. It is also a legal monument where are engraved, in the flesh and blood of patriots, the great realities of our times and the fine achievements of a group of men who want to give the world an example of sincere and active co-operation.
It is regrettable that Canada is not yet a member of the organization of American states. Already, invitations to become a member would have been possible; more recently, the trip of the ex-minister for external affairs again placed in the limelight the whole problem of our relations with the inter-American system, and the late Hon. Smith had stated at Rio de Janeiro and at Ottawa that the government would reconsider the case of the OAS and of Canada.
I earnestly wish that Canada will soon occupy the seat left vacant in the pan-American union because, in doing so, it would
116	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Herridge wholeheartedly play its due role, that of an intermediary between the old and the new world.
By belonging to the OAS, Canada would be in a much better position to explain to its neighbours of the other Americas and often to the United States, the role of the commonwealth in the world, as an instrument of peace and prosperity.
Our role in the OAS would be not only to protect Canadian interests, but also to achieve once again the co-ordination of those two great forces which are the commonwealth and the OAS. Also, in conferences grouping ministers of the British community, our country could explain and better bring home the power and value of the interAmerican system which, since 1889 has brought to our continent a policy of progress.
For too long, below the 45th parallel, has remained unnoticed the important work done by those great countries which are our friends to the south. And it is up to Canada to enshrine in history that conjunction of two great regional forces: the organization of American states and the commonwealth of nations. No other country possesses that double American and British nationality; no other country has, in such unique circumstances, the great advantage of having only friends in those two vast regional organizations. But in order to succeed in this delicate and important mission, Canada must belong fully and without second thoughts to those two organizations which it wants to bring together. This is a great mission, but Canada is certainly equal to the task.
