Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and to say we believe the structure of social justice can only be built upon the foundation of planned development of our resources, upon sound monetary, fiscal, investment and trade policies, upon co-operation between all levels of government and upon co-operation between these governments and the people.
We believe there has to be a much greater participation on the part of the people in the development of policies necessary to give us a sound economic structure in the future. We support wholeheartedly the limited response on the part of this government to the needs of the Canadian people at this time, but we are of the opinion that we cannot, shall I say, promote the sound improvement of our economic situation by this piecemeal, debt-creating approach.


We are referred to as socialists, I am quite proud to be known as a democratic socialist, but that does not mean to say we do not believe in sound economics. We believe two and two make four, and the way to provide all the necessary welfare benefits for the Canadian people, and the services they need, is to put people to work and have them producing goods and services rather than having them idle under present circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, I have limited time. I should like to speak at greater length on several aspects of the government's proposals at this time but I shall limit my remarks to practically one subject. We were all very interested in the mention made in the throne speech of a proposal for building a national power grid. Indeed, we were very pleased to see it mentioned in the speech because members of our group stressed the necessity for it some years ago. Trade unions have written to the Prime Minister and other cabinet ministers suggesting such a course of action and we are pleased to see at the least this mention of a proposal to build a national power grid because it offers an opportunity for the beginning of a well planned, long term development program. When I say "well planned" I mean something not entered into in a hurry but something planned over a period of years so that the investment to bring the project to completion can be undertaken without too great a burden on the Canadian economy.
At this stage I shall refer to the Columbia river situation, a subject which has been of great national, provincial and local interest. In my opinion, and that of the members of this group, the government made a mistake in signing the Columbia treaty prior to having an agreement in writing with the government of British Columbia. That, I think, goes without saying. It showed a lack of foresight. There was too great haste in signing it, and a lack of sufficient planning and acquisition of the facts required upon which to base a sound judgment at the time. Since then too there has been a lack of co-operation between the federal and provincial government, and between the provincial government and the persons directly or indirectly concerned.
I intended to have a lot to say about this, aspect Mr. Speaker, but I shall have to leave it and go on to deal with a particular angle of the whole matter. However, I cannot help just mentioning that the hearings held in Rev-elstoke, Nakusp, Kaslo and Castlegar attracted an attendance of some 1,000 supporters of the Columbia conservation confederation.

There were many supporters of the Conservative government amongst them. They belong to all parties. Regardless of political opinions we marched shoulder to shoulder on that occasion and some 300 people made verbal or written representations to the controller of water rights and expressed their objection to the building of the High Arrow dam. Objections were raised by the city of Revelstoke, and by the Arrow lakes water resources committee, by the women's institutes and farmers' institutes and by the chambers of commerce in southeastern British Columbia.
Objection has also been raised by the B.C. federation of labour, the mine, mill and smelter workers union-in fact, nearly all the unions in British Columbia-the British Columbia fish and game clubs and the resort operators' associations.
In addition to that, four professional engineers of well-known reputation gave testimony expressing their opposition to the building of this dam. Also, excellent briefs were presented that were designed to show the effect on the lives of some 2,000 people, on 18 communities, on the natural resources, recreational facilities, fish and game, and wildlife in general. Two excellent briefs were presented on the moral aspects of the present procedures and proposals, which I will deal with at a later date. One of these was by Dr. C. S. Fowler of Castlegar, and the other, I am very glad to say, was presented on behalf of the Anglican Lord Bishop of Kootenay, who expressed in strong language his attitude toward the undemocratic procedures and proposals in connection with this development. However, I must leave the details of that important matter until a later time.
I now come to this stalemate between the federal and provincial governments with respect to the Columbia river. Before I deal with some aspects of this question I wish to place on the record the position of this party.
We held a convention of the New Democratic party quite recently in British Columbia. At that convention the following resolution was adopted unanimously:
Power. Our cheapest source of power must be developed first. Available statistics suggest that this can be developed on the Columbia river. The New Democratic party favours the McNaughton plan which would eliminate the High Arrow dam project and the flooding of thousands of acres of valuable B. C. land. This low cost power must be used in British Columbia to create new industries and the thousands of new jobs which are required to expand our industrial production rapidly and to end mass unemployment in our province.
No firm or long term contracts should be made for the export of power or sale of downstream benefits from British Columbia.
The Address-Mr. Herridge
That resolution was adopted unanimously by the founding convention of the New Democratic party in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1961. The B.C. federation of labour met a few days previously. They have a research director for natural resources who understands the subject. He has a better knowledge of the subject of the conservation of natural resources and the natural resource problem in general than any official of the trade union movement I have met to date.
He studied this question and presented his views before the convention. As a result the B.C. federation of labour adopted unanimously a most interesting brochure on power and politics. If anybody wants to read it I am quite sure I can get copies for them. This is a responsible, thoughtful policy entitled "Power Resources Belong to the People". I do not have time to read it fully but I wish to deal very briefly with some of the conclusions. Among other suggestions are these three:
3.	Stop any plans which will mean the export of cheap Columbia power to the United States to the detriment of British Columbia's economic development.
4.	Development of the Columbia river project as soon as possible. Labour favours the McNaughton plan which would eliminate the High Arrow dam project and the flooding of thousands of acres of valuable B.C. land.
6. There must be full federal-provincial co-operation and planning in developing B.C.'s long term power needs. A national power grid system would guarantee cheap and plentiful electricity to provide for future domestic and industrial needs in an expanding economy.
Since that date the B.C. federation of labour have been so concerned about this matter that they sent a telegram to the Minister of Justice, dated November 24, 1961. This is what the telegram says:
The B.C. federation of labour opposes the export of power from British Columbia. Such a policy, we believe, will only lead to the further industrial development of the United States Pacific northwest and is tantamount to exporting jobs and industrial opportunities which under normal and proper development of the Columbia project would be provided for Canadians. We strongly urge the Canadian government under no circumstances to succumb to the pressures now being exerted by the Canadian chamber of commerce, the British Columbia Social Credit government and United States politicians for a reversal of the federal government's long standing policy on the question of power export.
That telegram is signed by Mr. R. R. Smeal, president, and Mr. E. P. O'Neal, secretary treasurer of the B.C. federation of labour.
In addition to that, quite recently Mr. Strachan, the leader of the New Democratic party in British Columbia who has been very concerned about this problem, issued a press

The Address-Mr. Herridge release. I am going to quote from it because we want to show where we stand on this important question. This is dated November 24, 1961, and reads as follows:
Power-Columbia river. For the second time in seven years the Social Credit government of B.C. is openly conspiring with U.S. interests to sell out the future development of this province for the immediate gain of a fast buck and to satisfy its political ambition.
The only justification for the Socred attitude is the hollow desire to humiliate both the present federal government and the previous Liberal federal government which had the courage to halt the Kaiser dam giveaway.
The present High Arrow dam scheme is nothing more than the old Kaiser dam deal in disguise. The Kaiser aluminum company's letter of April 2, 1958, written to a committee of the U.S. Senate (attached hereto), proves beyond doubt that Premier Bennett has always been obsessed with forcing on B.C. a type of Columbia development which is only second best. To get his way he has openly invited U.S. intervention into purely Canadian affairs.
The Social Credit government set out from the start of the present treaty negotiations to deliberately sabotage full economic development of the Columbia to provide the maximum possible benefit to Canada via the McNaughton plan.
The point has now been reached where the federal government must act to take all and any necessary steps to halt the present Social Credit plans, to propose alteration of the treaty to eliminate High Arrow, and to develop the Columbia for the benefit of Canadians, if necessary entirely under federal auspices.
I do not consider this an infringement of provincial rights. In fact I submit it is the right and indeed the duty of the federal government to protect the people of B.C. against this Social Credit government which has proved that it cannot be trusted to place the interests of its country before its own personal political ambition.
If the federal government fails to take this action they too will be guilty of betraying Canada's interests.
That is the position of the New Democratic party and of organized labour in British Columbia, whether they are unions affiliated with the Canadian Congress of Labour or independent unions. In order to bring into focus the attitude of the powers behind the scenes in British Columbia we should look at the attitude of Dr. Gordon Shrum who, as is known to anyone who knows what happens in British Columbia behind the scenes, is the real power behind power policy in British Columbia.
This gentleman has an excellent war record. He was decorated for bravery; he was awarded the O.B.E. He has an excellent record as an administrator and as a professor at the University of British Columbia. This is what he has to say, according to Bill Fletcher of the Vancouver Sun in an article appearing in that newspaper on Friday, August 25, 1961:
said Dr. Gordon Shrum, "couldn't care less about the Columbia".

Dr. Shrum, the approachable, outspoken chairman of the B.C. Electric Company and the B.C. energy board, meant simply this: The government and the big utility company it now owns are committed to development of the Peace river.
They are satisfied with the economics of generating power on the north central B.C. river and transmitting it 600 miles to the lower mainland.
They are content that they have out-foxed both Ottawa and Washington. And, if nothing is ever done to unsnarl the complications on the Columbia it won't matter a ruddy kilowatt to the people of this province.
A confident Dr. Shrum outlined his views on the future power picture for me this week.
That statement has not been denied to date. I emphasize again that these are the words of Dr. Shrum. If hon. members know who Dr. Shrum is in British Columbia they will realize that there is a lot behind these words.
I wish to make some comments about a speech by Dr. Keenleyside who is a member of the energy board of British Columbia and chairman of the B.C. power commission. I might say that some members of the press gallery and some persons who have been associated with Dr. Keenleyside in the United Nations and in various government departments tell me he operates the best personal publicity bureau of any civil servant in Canada. I know something of his very effective publicity through the public relations division of the B.C. hydro commission. Anyway, he has made a speech and distributed it widely across Canada. Moreover he is available, I understand, according to information given to me to Canadian clubs and other groups. He is quite willing to address them on this question and to place his views before them.
First of all, I wish to say that I am one who takes strong exception to employees of the public in the civil service or those who are heads of bodies such as the hydro commission making public statements on highly controversial issues. Those are matters which should be dealt with by the elected representatives of the people and by the people themselves. I have read Dr. Shrum's views. Dr. Keenleyside takes a different view and as I have said before he has been voicing his opinions by making speeches to any appropriate group which has been willing to listen.
Now I should like to make a few comments on the text of the speech which was made by Dr. Keenleyside on December 15, 1961. This speech was made in Nanaimo. I quote:
To the extent that our power problems are political in character I shall have no comment to make although, in present circumstances, any discussion of these problems may have political implications. But any such implications will be

incidental to my argument. Like everyone else, I have views on public matters, but I have taken no part in past political controversies and I have no intention of doing so now.
That is the understatement of the year. In fact, in my opinion, Dr. Keenleyside as a public employee and servant of the people is improperly engaged in one of the sharpest political controversies between governments in recent years.
Further on, as reported at page 5 of his speech, Dr. Keenleyside had this to say:
Nevertheless, low costs of large quantities of firm power are still important factors in deciding on the location of industry and the growth of population. Thus it is of the very first importance that British Columbia should have available quantities of power adequate to meet every foreseeable demand and at a price that will stimulate that demand.
Every industrial enterprise and every prospective settler should be aware that the cost of power in B.C. is at least as low as it is anywhere else on the continent. This has never been true in the past; it can and should be made true in the very near future. Any development program that does not aim directly at this target should be discarded.
Dr. Keenleyside, according to his speech, proposes to reach this target by selling Canadian power in the United States over a long period of years. I just mention this in order to show the contradiction in his argument. He continues, as appears on page 6:
The energy board indicated that the Peace could meet incremental loads of about 1,750 mw up to about 1975-78 and Columbia could meet incremental loads of about 2,500 mw up to about 1978-83. Thus well before 1985 the initial plans for these two rivers will have to be expanded or other sources developed to meet our domestic needs alone.
In that statement he puts the Peace ahead of the Columbia. He goes on to say as appears on pages 6 and 7:
It is appreciated that the cost of coal in Alberta is relatively low and so long as thermal plants can be constructed at the load centres there may not be large markets for the export of power from British Columbia. Nevertheless, the Alberta authorities are already showing an interest in Columbia power, and if, as was pointed out earlier, the costs of thermal power increase, our hydro generation, in spite of transmission costs, may soon become competitive in Alberta . . . But an interprovincial tie might well prove to be mutually advantageous. This will be particularly true if the present experimentation in high voltage, long distance, low cost transmission techniques proves successful, as Russian, Swedish and New Zealand tests seem to suggest.
The dream of a national network may be much nearer than was anticipated even three years ago. It is a dream that we all should seek to turn into reality.
However, although Dr. Keenleyside talks of Alberta showing an interest in Columbia power, he would prevent this development occurring for many years by selling surplus power in the United States on a firm basis over a long period of years. He continues:
This does not, of course, apply to the sale of downstream benefits which are not exports and
The Address-Mr. Herridge
the sale of which is permitted under the terms of the Columbia treaty signed by Ottawa and Washington.
Article 5 of the treaty provides that Canada is entitled to one half the downstream power benefits and that the United States shall deliver to Canada at the boundary this amount, less a transmission loss and amounts disposed of under Article 8, which provides that by exchange of notes a portion of this power can be sold in the United States.
However, without a doubt, the basic purpose of the treaty is to provide large quantities of cheap power and, in so doing, benefit the people of British Columbia as a whole through industrial development and the increased employment which will result. Undoubtedly, this purpose would be defeated and Canadians placed at a competitive disadvantage if the bulk of low cost downstream power were committed to the United States on a firm basis for a lengthy period as suggested by Dr. Keenleyside.
To continue, he goes on to say as reported on page 8:
Informal discussions have been held over the past year with agencies and organizations in the United States and we now know that a solid market exists for firm power at an attractive price.
This statement has never been proved to date and no one can say that it is a fact at this time. To continue the quotation:
If the Peace river power is not at first completely utilized in Canada some part of it could be offered to the United States at Blaine for about 5 mills.
Dr. Keenleyside here is suggesting that the Peace river is to have the whole Vancouver market with the intention of selling the downstream benefits to the United States over a long period of years. Then he continues, as appears on pages 10 and 11:
The terms of our agreements will not be 80 years but from 15 to 25 years, and the agreements will provide specific assurances that the power can be repatriated at the end of the contract term. This has already been publicly accepted by the U.S. authorities.
Well, anyone knows that if we sell firm power over a period of 15 to 25 years to the United States experience has proved that they build industries, they build communities based on that power, and it will never be recaptured by Canada.
Further on he says on page 11:
During the ten years, 1950-1960, there have been deliveries of firm power to the United States from Canada of about 150,000 kilowatts to 176,000 kilowatts each year.

The latest I have read is that in the first instance they would not sign a contract for power unless it is over a very lengthy period and on a firm basis, and I suggest that experience proves that when you sell power over a lengthy period you cannot recapture it. There is discussion in United States newspapers about the industries that can be established on the basis of this power. Dr. Keenleyside goes on to say on page 11:
During the ten years, 1950-1960, there have been deliveries of firm power to the United States from Canada of about 150,000 kilowatts to 176,000 kilowatts each year. These figures represent a little over half of one per cent of the total net generating capability of Canada today.
My comment in that respect is that Dr. Keenleyside fails completely to mention that all of these deliveries are on a short term basis and in some cases on an interruptable basis. I quote from page 13:
Sometimes it is a temptation to believe that there is some proof in the stories that one hears from time to time about the determination of influential interests in Ontario and Quebec to protect certain schemes or plans of their own by preventing the federal government from allowing British Columbia to use its power resources to maximum value.
By "maximum value" he means sales to the United States. Maximum use for British Columbia power resources is to sell the surplus power to Canadians. This seems to be an attempt on his part, in my opinion, to raise the old east versus west bogey, which I think is a most unfortunate approach. On the same page he says further:
Among our own people the fear has been expressed that a sale in the United States of our downstream benefits, as provided in the treaty, will mean that we would be selling cheap power to the Americans instead of bringing it home to use ourselves. If this were true I should certainly be among the first to oppose it. But, except in a very limited and temporary sense, it is not true.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this again is a complete distortion of the facts. Dr. Keenleyside knows it is true. He participated in all discussions that were held here in Ottawa during which there was never a hint of such a policy with respect to the sale of downstream benefits. Then, on page 14 of his speech he says:
The United States would get about 1 million kilowatts by making new expenditures which would be the equivalent of one mill per kilowatt hour.

I have discussed this with engineers, Mr. Speaker, and, of course, Dr. Keenleyside does not know this. I turn to page 15 where he
says:
B.C. could provide for its own needs by developing the Peace and paying a little over 4 mills for Peace power.
Without a doubt 4 mills is low. This is the key to the situation. It is in my opinion, to force Peace river power on British Columbia and keep out Columbia power and sell it in the United States. On page 16 Dr. Keenleyside says:
It was, of necessity, a compromise document and, on the whole, it gives Canada a return which a few years ago would have been discarded as a quite Utopian fantasy.
Here is my comment on that. This return was not to be on the basis of the sale of power in the United States. It was to be on the basis of cheap power delivered to the Canadian border. Then, I turn to page 18 where he says:
And who can say with complete assurance that the federal government will continue to refuse to give Victoria the same kind of assistance that it is giving Regina in the case of the South Saskatchewan dam?
Talk about not entering into political controversy, Mr. Speaker. In the first instance, the projects are not comparable, in my opinion, and in the second instance, this is a highly political statement on the part of Dr. Keenleyside and I think an improper statement coming from an employee of the people of British Columbia. He is our servant and he needs to remember that. I quote from page 19:
We should ... as soon as sale contracts can be negotiated in the United States proceed to the immediate development of the Columbia river treaty projects with a view to obtaining the first financial returns from the sale of the downstream benefits at the earliest possible moment-hopefully 1965.
In my opinion and in the opinion of a good many persons with whom I have discussed this matter, this policy is a complete sell-out of our power resources to the United States.

I am sorry to have taken the time of the house but I am very concerned and feel very deeply about this

matter, and I represent the views of a lot of my constituents and many other Canadians.
While the United States will appreciate this additional power and the flood control that this treaty will provide, no mention has been made to date of the even greater value of this enormous quantity of water for irrigation and other purposes. Friends of mine in the United States came to see me and informed me that already a number of pipes of huge diameter are being installed above Grand Coulee dam and plans are being made for the irrigation of hundreds of thousands of acres. We can use this water to irrigate hundreds of thousands of acres in the Okanagan in British Columbia.
In the future power can be obtained from a number of sources, but with the increase of population water will become an ever scarcer and more valuable commodity. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge the government to take advantage of the present situation to:
1.	Renegotiate the treaty and in so doing make the Mica Creek dam the heart of the development on the Columbia and eliminate the High Arrow dam with its unnecessary destruction of natural resources, communities and a large amount of public and private investment. We can at the same time provide our friends in the United States with ample stored water, flood control and so on.
2.	Preserve this million acre park intact with its abundance of recreational, fish and game resources.
3.	Establish a river basin agency which should represent the various interests in the basin. The primary impact of a water resources development and management program is on the people of the region affected. To date they have simply been told what is going to happen to them by their servants. The influence of water development is widely felt on agriculture, on forestry, on industry, on recreation and on fish and game resources. Such a development has a pronounced effect on the physical characteristics of the area in which all the residents have rights and important interests. Therefore, it is essential that the basin agency should represent the populace generally in the same manner as a legislator would represent them in other fields.
4.	Proceed immediately to promote the development of a national power grid in order that surplus power from the Columbia would be used to develop Canadian industry and promote employment.
5.	Promote an appreciation and understanding on the part of the public generally of this vast project and so enlist the co-operation of the people and their organizations.
The Address-Mr. Nielsen
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say this. Let our motto be: Use Canadian power to develop Canadian industry and, second, use Canadian water to develop Canadian agriculture. I urge the government to seize the opportunity presented by this stalemate to promote the planned development of our resources to the advantage of all Canadians. I thank hon. members for their consideration.

I should like to add my congratulations to those extended to the mover (Mr. Bourdages) and the seconder (Mr. Browne, Vancouver-Kingsway) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne as well as to those extended to the newly appointed Deputy Speaker and the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Flynn).
I intend to answer some of the charges made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and others who have spoken from the other side of the chamber, by dealing with two departments with which I have endeavoured to make myself familiar while I have been here, namely the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and, just as important, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
When I first arrived here it was a surprise and a source of wonderment to me that the federal government could go along for so many years without recognizing the necessity for creating a department of forestry inasmuch as the activities of such a department would undoubtedly increase the economic stature of Canada. The second matter that surprised me was the fact that such little attention was being paid to the activities of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys having regard to the fact that the mineral industry in Canada latterly has been responsible for some 40 per cent to 42 per cent of our total exports. In the time during which I have been here it has been the practice of hon. members opposite to adopt the attitude of scorning the expressed policy of the government of developing Canada as a whole rather than as a group of ten provinces. I refer particularly to the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) who I am sorry to note is not in his seat but who cannot go without mention, as well as another absent member, namely the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets). These members and many more like them on the opposite side of the chamber tend to look upon Canada as it is often described, namely as a narrow ribbon of population stretching from the Atlantic across to the Pacific. They forget completely that well over 40 per cent of the nation's resources lie above the boundary line of the sixtieth parallel.

The Address-Mr. Nielsen
The resources of the north have always been a challenge. They have always constituted a potential which, if attacked with vigour, imagination and vision, would produce for Canada an economic impetus which would be felt in a corresponding rate of growth in our national economy. It seems to me that the Leader of the Opposition and those who support him look not to national development in terms of the development of natural resources in a national sense but rather to the development of measures which are calculated to impress those more highly populated areas of Canada in which of course, a greater number of votes are to be reached. In this consideration perhaps lies the secret of 22 years of Liberal tenure when the north, in the language of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), stagnated. In those years, Mr. Speaker, little was done in the way of vigorous, imaginative and aggressive development of the resources heritage which belongs to all Canadians and which lies within the confines of this vast part of Canada. However, one needs only to make comparison.
It is all very well for hon. gentlemen opposite to attack the policies of the party of the north. That is indeed what this party is, but not in the sense that it expects to gain votes for developing the north; for in that area constituting 40 per cent of Canada there are only two seats, namely the one for Yukon and the one for Mackenzie River. Hence one cannot confront the government with the accusation that they are attempting to garner votes by putting national funds into the development of northern resources. The common sense conclusion must be that the government is making a sincere endeavour to develop these resources for the benefit of the whole of the nation.
It is easy for the Leader of the Opposition to say that what is required are wise and farsighted plans and policies-I believe those were his words-with leadership which puts national interest above party advantage. Surely the Leader of the Opposition cannot accuse the government of putting party advantage above the national interest when the professed intention of the government is to develop the resources of the northern areas which are represented, in terms of seats in the House of Commons, by two out of 265. I ask hon. members opposite, Mr. Speaker, if they really believe the words of their leader when they accuse this government of putting party advantage before national interest when they follow the aggressive, enlightened and vigorous policy of developing the north and when the intention must be that of promoting the national interest and only that?

Mr. Speaker, before we adjourned I had mentioned that there were two points in the speech from the throne to which I wished to refer as they are of particular interest to me. One is the provision which parliament will be asked to make for an expanded program of encouragement of scientific research in Canada, a provision which I should like to believe is the result of the work of the special committee on research which was established last year. It is, I believe, the responsibility of government to expend moneys in partnership with private industry particularly in the field of applied research so that the facilities of governmental agencies, especially those of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, are made available to fundamental research.
The other provision in the speech from the throne to which I wish to refer is the subject of a bill which I have introduced this session concerning representation in the Senate, and I will simply refer to that by expressing the hope that the measure concerned will make provision for representation in the Senate for the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
Before the dinner adjournment I was drawing comparisons, and I should like to refer very briefly to the fact that I put on record in Hansard last session a table of comparative statistics as to the amount expended on investment in northern development in the five years prior to 1957 and the amount expended in the four or four and a half years subsequent to 1957. In most cases the investment was multiplied five times and in many cases it was tenfold.
In answer to those who are critical of the progress which is being made in the northern development program, I have some figures here from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. For the fiscal year 1956-57 federal expenditures on road

construction and maintenance in both the Yukon and Northwest Territories amounted to $2,655,000. In the current fiscal year the estimates provide for $9,278,000. I should explain that the final figure for expenditures is not available since all the accounts are not in, but the program is proceeding according to schedule. To me this increase in federal investment in Canada's northern areas is indicative of those wise and planned policies to which the Leader of the Opposition was referring yesterday in his remarks, expenditures which I think I should say were completely overlooked when he and his colleagues formed the government.
In total the votes for work in the north administered by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources have grown from $11,318,000 in 1956-57 to $36,536,000 in 1961-62. The resultant stimulation of prospecting which will undoubtedly bring about a greater and more rapid exploitation of the nation's mineral wealth in the northern areas of our country cannot, in my view at any rate, be overemphasized.
A more startling comparison, however, exists with regard to oil and gas exploration activity in the areas north of the sixtieth parallel. The total number of leases, permits and reservations in good standing in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon is 2,133 covering 106,680,022 acres. Compare this with the January, 1957, total of 12 million acres under permit in addition to about 6 million acres in the two reservations in the Yukon territory and the small proven field at Norman Wells.
Since major oil and gas exploration got under way in 1957, about $56 million has been spent. Between now and 1970 indications are that a further $300 million will be spent and the total may well go far beyond this. Information at the present time about plans for the coming year indicates that expenditures of the order of $15 million will be made over the next 12 months. I will not bore the house by including the breakdown of the permits, leases and reservations which are now in good standing in the territories. Suffice it to say that it is as a direct result of the oil and gas policies of the government that such a large expansion in the stimulation of oil and gas exploration in the northern areas of Canada has come about.
Passing to the activities of the mines and technical surveys department, again I refer to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition when he said that what is required is wise and planned policies, farsighted plans and policies with leadership which puts national interest above party advantage. Again I em-
The Address-Mr. Nielsen phasize the point that the policies that the government is following in the development of these northern areas of our nation cannot be held to be anything less than in the national interest, particularly in view of the remarks that the Leader of the Opposition and his colleagues have made time and time again criticizing the government for making these large investments in Canada's north rather than making them in the more populated, vote-catching areas of the south. I submit it is in the national interest of those opposite that this nation be developed as a whole and not region by region.
A brief glance at the economic situation relative to the mineral industry in the country provides, I think, some very startling comparisons. Canadian mineral production in 1957 was valued at $2.1 billion, with metallic minerals accounting for $1.1 billion and industrial minerals accounting for $442 million and mineral fuels $555 million. Per capita value of mineral output was $128.64. The seasonally adjusted index of physical volume of the mineral industry was 235.8, with the index set in 1949 at 100, and the index for the industry as a whole in 1957 was 148.6.
Canadian mineral production in 1960 is valued at $2.5 billion, with metallic minerals accounting for $1.45 billion, industrial minerals $480 million and mineral fuels $570 million. Per capita value of mineral output is estimated at $140. The seasonally adjusted index of physical volume of the mineral industry is estimated at 257, and the index for the industry as a whole in 1960 is estimated at 169.
In the three year period from 1957 to 1960, the total value of mineral production increased $400,000, or 19 per cent, averaging a little more than 6 per cent per year. The index of physical volume for the industry in that period increased from 235.8 to an estimated 257.0, or 8.5 per cent.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that the value of our mineral exports was 40 to 42 per cent of the total value of the nation's export trade. Exports of minerals and products based on the mineral industry in 1950 were valued at $812 million. The value of the total exports in that year was $3,118 million.
Exports of minerals and mineral-based products, for the first nine months of 1957 and 1960 were valued at $1,521.5 million and $1,718.9 million respectively. Total Canadian exports in 1957 and 1960 were valued at $3,570 million and $3,899.6 million respectively, and on this, Mr. Speaker, the conclusion can be made that minerals and mineral-based products accounted for approximately

The Address-Mr. Nielsen 44 per cent of total exports in the first nine months of 1960, up from 42 per cent in the like period of 1957, and 26 per cent for the 1950 calendar year. The importance of the mineral industry to the nation's economy, I submit, cannot be overemphasized.
The sum total of mineral products on a comparison basis will be illustrated when I say that iron and its products exported in 1957 accounted for $392.8 million, or 11 per cent of the total, while in 1960 they accounted for $464.9, or 12 per cent of the total. Nonferrous metals and their products brought in $742.8 million in 1957, which was 20.8 per cent of our total exports, and in 1960 they brought in $920.6 million or 23.6 of the total. In fact, exports of mineral products increased all along the line from 1957 to 1960, and I believe that the increase is in a large measure attributable to expanded activity in the development of natural resources brought about by the policies of this government.
We have been criticized by the opposition for not taking any action. We have been criticized by the hon. member for Assiniboia for stagnation in the development of the nation's natural resources, but let us have a look at the facts in so far as the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is concerned.
Action taken relative to the development of the north started in 1958 with a $6 million photographic project of the Arctic. Second, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has recognized a definite need to secure additional information about the resources potential of the Queen Elizabeth islands area of Canada. This region may be a valuable future potential source of oil and minerals. The department has therefore organized and dispatched a research team of 60 professional and sub-professional personnel to the area, and this group has produced valuable practical information which will be essential to the ultimate development of the resources of the Arctic islands.
Third, shoran geodetic control work was completed in 1958 for the Arctic islands and fourth, a program of accurate topographic mapping of the Arctic islands, which will continue for four or five years, was commenced.
The fifth point is that in co-operation with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources a survey is proceeding of localities in northern Canada which may serve as sites for new communities. Sixth, preliminary surveys for power facilities on the Yukon river have recently started.
The seventh point in the program is that geological work in the north has been greatly increased since 1957 in accordance with the

expressed government policy of developing Canada's northland. The eighth step was the launching of geographical surveys in northern Canada, which are now under way in cooperation with the department of northern affairs, to help develop the economy of surveyed areas and assist local Indian or Eskimo populations.
Surveys are proceeding towards new locations or relocations of settlements in northern Canada, and the tenth point is that an intensified program has been undertaken of recording the earth's magnetism and magnetic storms, particularly in northern Canada to assist navigation, surveying and geophysical prospecting. Is that indicative of a lack of wise planning and policies? Things that should have been done long ago are now being undertaken by this government to develop a part of Canada which for years and years was forgotten and which, in the words of the hon. member for Assiniboia "stagnated" under the rule of the Liberal regime.
What about the roads to resources program?

My friend the hon. member for Ottawa West, interjects from his seat, as his colleagues are wont to do from time to time, and if I had not asked him to repeat his question I would not have heard it. Well, there have been more bridges built than the bridge at Prince Albert and remember, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals were speaking for years and years about the Saskatchewan river dam project. The Liberals have been speaking about roads and bridges all across the country but there had to be a different government come in to do what the Liberals were only talking about.
Sound action has been taken by the mines and technical surveys department in relation to the roads to resources program. A very significant contribution to the roads to resources program is being made by the geological survey of Canada in connection with surveys over 60,000 square miles of potential

mineral territory in northwestern Ontario. Commercial aircraft are being employed to assist in the aerial work. This type of program provides the opportunity of working with the provinces in developing new techniques in prospecting on a regional scale. The geochemical work, in particular, may have broad applications to mineral exploration in Canada. Already, prospecting has been stimulated in northwestern Ontario as a result of this activity in mineral exploration. The aeromagnetic maps prepared by the geological survey of Canada and the Ontario department of mines are being distributed and are aiding considerably in encouraging mineral industry activity.
The geological survey is actively continuing its program of aeromagnetic survey work through Canada and makes maps quickly available to assist in the search for new mineral deposits.
Officers of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys have been responsible for mineral resource appraisals in connection with all proposed road programs across Canada since the establishment of the roads to resources program, a program which was initiated by this government and talked about for many years by those opposite.
Before my time expires I wish to deal very quickly with the federal contribution made in respect of the development of social services in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, that part of Canada which I again say constitutes 40 per cent of the nation's wealth and resources-perhaps even more than that.
In the Yukon territory federal contributions were made to schools in the following amounts: to the Destruction bay school $45,500; to the Takhini school, $214,500. This is still under negotiation. The Watson lake school, $72,865; to the Selkirk street school, $149,370; to the new high school, $367,188 of $1J million. Negotiations are still going on there. The federal government is contributing 75 per cent of the estimated total cost of the new vocational school in the amount of $743,000. To the separate schools program there were grants of $162,000 and $40,000 in those years.
The federal contribution to education in the Northwest Territories was $5,036,987 in 1957-58; $5,059,486 in 1958-59; $3,910,314 in 1959-60, and $2,240,514 in 1960-61, with a gross expenditure of $16,247,301 since this government took office. There is a forecast for 1962 of well over $2 million.
The same story can be told throughout federal department after federal department having anything to do with the north. Where 26207-1-9
The Address-Mr. Matheson before you had a complete absence of attention to the north-indeed, a complete neglect-you have now a sincere and a very well meaning intention to develop Canada's northland to the benefit of the nation.
I can point out several small indications, such as the Prime Minister's visit to the Yukon territory and the Northwest Territories, which areas for the first time in Canada's history were visited by a Canadian prime minister. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) said during the last session that he visited Canada's northland. I said then, and I say again,-and I challenge him now that I see him in his seat-to tell us when he did visit the northland. If he indeed did travel above the sixtieth parallel he certainly did not look around him to see what potential this area of Canada had to offer to the economic development of the whole nation.
What action has the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys taken relative to applied research in the mineral resource development of this nation? In the first place, the practice followed over the years of assisting the mineral industry by laboratory research projects carried out in the mines branch laboratories has been accelerated during the past two or three years. Projects are carried on at the specific request of companies and also in line with fundamental research plans of the department directed toward greater development and utilization of Canada's mineral resources. In particular, stress is being laid on techniques which will lead to further processing of minerals in Canada, something which I submit was entirely overlooked for many, many years by those opposite.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address myself to one of the most urgent and certainly most ignored problems in Canada, the plight of the dairy farmer. Before doing so I wish to join in the congratulations to both the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
(Translation):
I should like to offer my congratulations to the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Flynn) on his recent appointment. I have been closely acquainted with the other distinguished member for the constituency of Quebec South, Hon. C. G. Power, who is a great Canadian and who successively held four portfolios. Although the present Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys does not belong to the same party as Mr. Power, I suggest that he take him as his model.

The Address-Mr. Matheson
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, the seconder of the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) concluded his remarks with these words:
By any analysis of our economy and its future prospects there is no cause for pessimism. By any analysis whatever there is every reason for all Canadians to move forward to a greater and brighter future under the brilliant leadership of the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, one of the world's outstanding leaders.
I should like to refer to the language used by the Prime Minister in the opening campaign speech at Massey hall on April 25, 1957, which is very much in the minds and memories of us all. He said:
We will assure the farmer of his fair share of the national income by maintaining a flexible .. . price support program to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers based on a fair price-cost relationship... It represents in general the viewpoint of organized agriculture across Canada. It represents the experience of every other country with free economy in agriculture. It represents the need at this time if agriculture is to take its proper place in this nation.
I will now read from the Ontario Union Farmer of January, 1962, page 1, an article entitled "Promises of the Government":
These are the written words of the Conservative government and we quote further-"Canada now has a Prime Minister and a government who are not only greatly concerned about the farmer's position in our national economy but are determined that everything possible will be done to place agriculture in its proper position in that economy".
Then the editor says:
Lately there has been a considerable selling campaign in action to promote the idea that the present government has fulfilled all their promises to agriculture and to the farmers concerned.
Thank goodness we have a few people in farm union ranks, at least, to challenge these statements.
Then the article continues:
In view of the fact that inflation was not checked, the dollar value remains near the half way mark, and there is certainly no justification to say that farm people enjoy the degree of equality promised and advocated for years by our present Prime Minister.
I should like to refer this house to a few figures, the latest that I have been able to obtain from the Ontario department of agriculture. These figures refer to total standard fluid and special fluid milk bought and they are for Leeds county: $4.86 a cwt. for special fluid milk and $2.51 for secondary milk, or an average of $4.23. If we look at the figures for the years 1960 and 1961 we see prices dropping substantially. There was a drop from $2.60 to $2.53 in 1960-61, or a decrease in the average from $4.59 to $4.52.
What about the cost of products? I am referring to the latest figures available to us for products delivered, via Ottawa, November 1960-1961. For oats delivered, Ottawa, the price was $62 per ton. A year later it was $67.80. With respect to barley the price
[Mr. Matheson.)
was $54.25 in 1960 and it went up to $62.50 in 1961. For bran the price was $50.25 in 1960 and it went up to $54 in 1961. For shorts the price was $52.35 in 1960 and it went up to $57 in 1961. For dry and freshening feeds the price was $73.25 in 1960 and it went up to $77.25 in 1961.
I read from the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 20, 1957:
For the farmers Mr. Diefenbaker pledged a fair share of the national economy through a flexible support price program to ensure parity between farm prices and costs.
At St. Patrice de Beaurivage at the beginning of his campaign the Prime Minister spoke on the same subject.
(Translation) :
Speaking on the same subject, Mr. Diefenbaker added: "We recognize that the farmers' prosperity is the basic condition for the general prosperity of this country. The reforms we advocate can be summed up as follows: reasonable prices by means of price support, and substantial markets for your products."
(Text):
Let me refer to some of the figures I was able to get just today about the price index. I think we heard the Prime Minister tell us he was maintaining the value of the Canadian dollar. If this is so it certainly does not prevail with respect to some of our people in farming constituencies. These figures refer to commodities used by farmers and I am taking first the figure in August, 1957, which was 241. In 1962 the latest figure available was 262.4, an increase of 10 per cent. If we take out the living component we find that in August, 1957 the figure was 257.6 whereas now it is 287.8.
If we turn now to the consumer price index we find that in November 1956 it was 120.3. The figure in 1961, the latest figure available, was 129.7.
One of the last things which Mr. Grant Dexter wrote before he died was a series of articles which he called "Fountain Pen Money" as a result of the fiscal and monetary policies adopted by this government. These are matters we can fairly bring to the attention of the house and of the public. An article which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on September 11, 1961 was headed "Costs in Canada, U.S., Higher, Rising Faster Than Elsewhere: Study". The Montreal Gazette on December 7 carried an article headed "Living Cost Index up Half-Point to Record". On October 6, 1961 the Ottawa Citizen carried a story pointing out the cost of living in Canada was rising higher and higher.
Leeds is a typical dairy county with 30,000 milk cows and an annual production of 180 million pounds of milk. I would say that between three-fifths and nine-tenths of all the land stretching from Leeds to the Quebec border in Glengarry is used for dairy farming.

These are old settlements-the oldest and proudest U.E.L. settlements in Canada-and it will not do to tell these people to move off the land or to grow trees.
But all Canada is interested in this dairy problem. Ontario is by no means the only province which is interested in this solution. I recall to the house that in Ontario important fluid milk shippers are established at Halton, Ontario, Lincoln, Essex, Haldimand and Sim-coe. Processed milk shippers are established in Oxford, Elgin, Perth, Huron, Hastings and Prince Edward. I invite representatives of dairy constituencies to stand up and be counted now, in their speeches in this house as well as in caucus, because the dairy industry is in trouble and it is about time parliament recognized some of the facts.
I stress the lead that Ontario must give, because 37 per cent of all fluid sales in Canada come from the province of Ontario. This is not a small business. This is a billion dollar business with 350,000 farm families and as many in the other branches of the industry, such as processing and marketing, dependent upon it. I may say we have 50,000 fewer dairy farmers today than we had ten years ago so it is not a case of this constituency growing; it is a case of this constituency now being in serious trouble.
May I refer now to some figures prepared by the economics department, Ontario Agricultural College. First, dairy specialty farms. This refers to a particular group of people, the producers of fluid milk. After making allowances for expenses and the interest on capital the net income from labour amounts to $3,027. There were 156 farms included in the survey made of that grade. Fifteen low labour income farms which were also surveyed showed an annual loss under this labour income item of $2,035. I ask any fair minded person in parliament: how would you like to have $30,000 tied up in a farm in order to earn an income from labour of $3,000? The Prime Minister spoke to an audience on May 16, 1957 and said that the farmer was the forgotten man in Canada's boom. I say now that the dairy farmer is the forgotten man in Canada's recession.
I turn now to refer to the report entitled "Dairy General". This deals with the people who sell to the processing plants. Here we see yet another picture. One hundred and twenty eight farmers stated their receipts, their expenses and the money left as operators' income. The final figure, net labour income, amounted to $1,212 a year. That amounts to 30 cents an hour for his labour for a man supplying milk to a manufacturing milk plant. I remind the house of the Prime Minister's promise that something would be 26207-1-91
The Address-Mr. Matheson done to assist the Canadian farmer who, he said, had been relentlessly squeezed between declining prices for his products and rising living costs. Well, never has the situation been as serious as that which affects the dairy farmer today.
Without a sound and healthy dairy industry there cannot be a sound rural economy in a great many sections of Canada. This is the most widespread industry in the country and it affects the livelihood of many people in every province. Any policy we adopt must be national in its scope. This is a complicated problem and it is one whose solution calls for the most careful study and analysis because conditions which prevail in one part of the country do not prevail in another.
For example, 50 per cent of prairie milk goes into butter and skim milk powder. Ninety per cent of the cheese is made from Ontario and Quebec milk. British Columbia is the only province where 50 per cent of the milk produced is used as whole milk. This situation makes a national policy difficult to formulate. Some of the figures I intend to read now will, however, make the situation clearer to hon. members. First, I think it is important to note where the milk produced in Canada goes. The amounts of milk going into various outlets are approximately as follows:
Butter and skim milk powder		42 per cent
Whole milk and cream	 31 per cent
Condensed products and ice cream 9 per cent
Cheese	 7 percent
Farm butter and milk used on farms 11 per cent
100 per cent
This means that 73 per cent of production goes into two outlets which return over 80 per cent of the total cash income for the whole industry. Our policy, as a national policy, should, surely, be directed toward expanding these two largest sources of income, but this is not the case.
Our problem is that the consumption of butter is declining at a rate which is creating a serious situation, one which is frightening well informed people in the agricultural industry today.
A second serious point is that whole milk consumption is not keeping pace with our increase in population; for some years we have seen a regular decline in consumption per capita. What is going to happen very shortly is that this basic industry will collapse. A national policy must reverse both the trends I have mentioned. We must consume far more dairy products, particularly butter and whole milk. It is essential that this should be done and it should be tackled on a national basis because nothing else will be sufficient.

The Address-Mr. Matheson
One might say that there is another solution, namely, to cut production. However, this is not a solution which we on this side of the house would favour. We may leave it to the wisdom of some of these agricultural people who have done a lot of research on this question and who have suggested for example the introduction of a reduced lactation period, unified marketing plans within provinces, etc., all designed to control overproduction. But a national policy should be directed to increasing consumption immediately.
The promised land, the supreme gift of God, was, according to the book of Joshua, a land flowing with milk and honey. The fact is that we are a severely depressed land stockpiled with butter, and what is flowing is not milk. I was reading an article in the Rural Co-Operator of January 10 which indicated that beer consumption in the Toronto area increased by 12 per cent last year. I will read hon. members later an account of what happened to milk consumption in the same period.
Before getting to the heart of this problem may I offer the house some general facts that we should consider before enunciating a solution to the difficulties of this industry. Canada total milk production is estimated at 19.2 billion pounds, 4 per cent higher than in 1960. There has been a build-up in cow numbers since 1960 and this will possibly last through 1964. The numbers of milk cows on farms has increased in the five year period from 1957 to 1961 by 6.2 per cent in Ontario and by 5.6 per cent in Quebec, for a national average of 3.8 per cent.
Along with this increase in the cow population a great tendency has been noted to increase the size of commercial farms. There has certainly been an increase in efficiency, in technique, in ability to provide better pasturage. From 1948 to 1957 the number of cows on factory milk farms increased from 17 to 20 and on fluid milk farms from 23 to 30. The capital required for a factory milk farm now averages about $22,000 and for a fluid milk farm about $38,000.
One of our problems is the fact that the production per unit has increased substantially. The average last year was approximately 5,900 pounds per cow. One very large herd in Ontario had a production rate of over 10,000 pounds per cow right throughout the herd.
Now, is there a solution to this problem of current over-production? This over-production problem may only be with us for a few years. There is a solution. We have to deal with this butter situation. We have to face it now. We cannot put it off. I remind the house that the government had ample notice of this

problem. The dairy farmers and the Canadian federation of agriculture have made representations to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton). I recall reading an address which was delivered in the other place by a former provincial minister of agriculture, on January 24, 1961. This address was reprinted in a great many farm journals and a good many editorials. Nothing has been done. No attention has been paid to the problem. The present butter surplus is the direct result, Mr. Speaker, of this government succumbing to the temptation of promising before the last election that there would be a 64 cent floor price on butter, I say that with authority.
For three and a half years the government has watched the surplus build up until it is now a great depressant to the dairy industry. In this connection, I would tell the house that between 1949 and 1958, when there was a 58 cent price on butter, the domestic disappearance of butter increased year by year. The disappearance was 261 million pounds in 1949 and 322 million pounds in 1958 at the 58 cent floor price. In 1958, we had this pre-election offer of 64 cents, without any deficiency plan whatever, although many experts requested a deficiency plan in order to put butter on the market on the basis that would ensure its immediate use. Butter consumption started down in 1958 and has dropped every year since. We now have the situation of a very serious build-up of stocks, one that is worrying a great many experts.
I remind the house that Mr. Pierre Cote, who was president of the national dairy council, has, on several occasions, given addresses on this subject. He gave one on January 16, 1962, and I notice that he gave an important address on December 1, 1960, which was directed to the government. He has spoken on this subject repeatedly, asking that the government immediately take steps to get rid of this surplus which is actually depressing the value of all dairy products.
We on this side ask for an immediate consumer subsidy of 14 cents a pound so that butter can be put on the market at 50 cents per pound. Then it will be consumed before it is spoiled. There might be a little variation of this policy. There may be other ways by which this can be done, but we have to get that butter to the public at a price that will ensure its sale. I suggest that the government give consideration to the 50 cent figure. It might be that we could do this in other ways by means of deficiency payment, but we have to get rid of this butter. We have to get people back into the habit of consuming butter.
Our national goal should be the consumption of 20 pounds of butter per person per year. With 18 million people in this country,

this consumption rate would restore the balance. We are now consuming approximately 15.1 pounds per person. I might tell you that for many years we had a much larger rate of consumption of butter than this. I will refer, if I may a little later in my remarks, to some of the actual consumption rates by Canadians. There has been some popular chatter about cholesterol and heart disease. This question was handled by the former minister of agriculture to whom I have referred. He indicated that studies had been made in the United States which indicated the extent to which Canadians suffered from heart disease in comparison with the people of the United States who consumed far less butter. We know that the people of northern Ireland, Finland and New Zealand consume over 30 pounds per capita with a very slight incidence of heart disease. The United States has the highest incidence of heart disease in the world with a butter consumption of something over 6 pounds per person. There was a time when we, in Canada, consumed about 34 pounds of butter per person. I ask the house, therefore, to consider very seriously the question of whether or not the Department of Agriculture should give some thought to reversing this adverse publicity which is debasing our industry.
The next thing we have to consider is the problem of the consumption of fluid milk. There has been a steady downward trend in the consumption of fluid milk since 1956 when consumption was 314 pints per person per year. In 1961, the consumption per capita was around 302 pints. A comparison of the decline in fluid milk and cream since 1955 is even more startling. Canada must rapidly become milk conscious for the sake of national health as well as for the sake of the dairy industry. We do not dare compare this trend with the consumption of alcoholic beverages in the same period.
In our world of the dairy industry, a permanent cloud rests in the lowering of consumption of our milk products per capita. This consumption, which was 1,150 pounds per capita in 1950, has lowered to 940 pounds in 1960 whereas production remains at a base of 1,035 pounds. Our future markets will be established by the solution to the equation formed by a growing population but meanwhile progressively consuming less of our products. I say to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) that one of the ways we could do this would be to make milk available to our soldiers and to people in service hospitals. We should give them all the milk they can drink. I am sure those of you who were soldiers can remember how
The Address-Mr. Matheson much you would have liked to drink milk in large quantities. Then, what about the penitentiaries? What about making milk available to those people in some volume?
What about a school program? In the United States and in almost all parts of western Europe a school milk program is doing a great deal to alleviate this problem. Could we reverse the trend in this country with a school milk program? I say we could.
I was noticing again an article published in one of the newspapers showing what had been done in the Windsor area. The milk producers league increased the use of fluid milk by 6 per cent in one year through the institution of a school milk program. In England we have a situation where they are getting rid of milk in volume by the use of vending machines. The government is taking an active interest in this program and they have increased milk consumption by 10 per cent by this technique. It would not be difficult to adopt this program in Canada. We must make milk available to our armed forces, our hospitals, our penitentiaries and particularly our school children. We could do this and it would be the best thing we could do for the nation. In the United States, about 4 per cent of the fluid milk being used is being used by school children. In Canada, the figure is less than 1 per cent. There is nothing that will improve this rate of consumption like a consumer subsidy for the fluid product.
Then, what about strontium 90? We have heard a lot about strontium 90 in recent days because people are so conscious of what has been happening as a result of these tests in the atmosphere. There has been much adverse publicity lately about milk as a carrier of strontium 90. Although it is in all foods, greater publicity has been given to milk because of its purity and because milk samples are available at all times of the year in all parts of the country for purposes of tests. I think it is time the Canadian government took a special interest in making it clear to the people that the cow screens as much as seven eighths of the strontium 90 from her diet. We do not know how much strontium 90 is carried in wheat, cabbages, lettuce and other things because these tests are not easy to do. They are easy to do in connection with milk. Even the one eighth of the strontium 90 which remains in milk can be removed. Dr. B. B. Migicovsky, of the research branch of the Department of Agriculture has developed a technique whereby this can be done. Another important thing is this. If the human body has a choice between calcium and strontium 90, the tendency is for the body to discriminate against strontium 90 and to take

The Address-Mr. Matheson calcium. Our greatest source of supply for calcium is milk. In other words, in order to be safe from the hazards of strontium 90 a person should drink milk.
It is urgent that we build up our consumption of milk products, particularly, as I say, of butter and fluid milk. Gilbert MacMillan says that one of the most important means to this end is to have a federal standard for whole milk. I refer to the many submissions that have been put forward by him and other dairy experts who say that it is about time that we had a federal .standard for whole milk which would clearly define the fat and Splids-not-fat content of milk. Mr. MacMillan is well known to the Department of Agriculture. He was president of the Dairy Farmers of Canada and served on the National Dairy Council. He was president of the Canadian Ayrshire Breeders' Association. His opinions are studied all over the world and, I think it is about time that we studied them in Canada.
I wish to refer only briefly to the problems of our powdered skim milk people. I am referring to a few comments by Mr. Philippe Pariseault that he made a few days ago. He says this:
We have seen then from September to November, a movement without equal In export sales and the give away prices varying from 5 cents to 52 cents at port of embarking for spray process powdered milk and 4 cents to 4i cents for roller process milk powder. How can one cover costs at these prices?
These prices do not even cover the drying expenses. Consequently the producers have suffered very seriously.
One of our greatest products in the dairy industry is cheese. This is a matter in which we: are interested in Leeds county. I know that in years past you have heard George Fulford and Hayden Stanton speak about Leeds cheese. At the turn of the century we had 85 or 90 cheese factories in Leeds county. Today we have eight. Yet this is a product which the British would like on a premium basis if we could produce the kind of cheese they want in their market. All our experts tell us that there is a great market for mature quality Cheddar in the United States. They say there is there a potential market of tremendous importance.
* i One of the problems arises from the fact that modern techniques seem to go against getting the kind of flavour for which the farmers were famous years ago. Although I do not know this, maybe they were not quite as sanitary then, but at least they produced a product that was known all over the world. Today we have a great many tests. Refrigeration seems to do something to cheese as also does pasteurization. However, it is necessary for us to be much more interested m our
IMr. Matheson.]

cheese community. Hector Arnold who, I believe, has Conservative sympathies, has protested the regrading regulations. He says that exports have been held up. There is available an article to which the Minister of Agriculture might care to refer. It is to be found in the Rural Co-operator of January 16, 1962. He mentions the grading requirements at the moment which are doing a great deal to spoil our export sales to Britain.
I know that some thought is being given to the matter, particularly by new Canadians. In Leeds we have many Dutch people who are highly skilled in dairy matters. They have been able to teach us a great deal about techniques of their own. They are splendid farmers and some of these people are going to start to produce a Dutch cheese that we hope to put on the domestic market and thereby perhaps help in fighting this 13 million pounds of import of foreign type cheese that is coming into Canada because of people's taste preference.
I have not addressed myself to some of the other basic problems of this industry such as the matters discussed by Dr. David Mac-Farlane and other people who mention the disparity in price between fluid milk and manufactured milk. I think many of these problems are within the purview of the province or even of the industry itself. It is a responsible, wise and shrewd industry which has given a great deal of thoughtful advice to the Department of Agriculture. What we must do is rapidly build up demand. Today in Leeds, when a farmer needs to buy a coat for his wife or a tire for his truck, it is necessary for him to sell cattle because he cannot pay for these things out of his milk cheque; nor indeed in many cases can he pay his taxes or the interest on his mortgage. Some of our townships are falling very seriously behind in past due tax payments.

speechtext:
At
the present time, Mr. Speaker, we are debating the subamendment. If I read the subamendment in conjunction with the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), the two joined together would read somewhat in this way:
We respectfully affirm that Your Excellency's advisers, because of their continuing failure to bring forward policies to deal with the real problems confronting this country, including the failure-
Here I am quoting from the subamendment of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue).

-to promote the planned development of our resources, sound monetary, fiscal, Investment and trade policies which will develop our economy so as to provide:
1.	expanding export markets for agricultural and industrial production;
2.	full employment;
3.	and, in co-operation with the provinces, a prepaid medical care program for all Canadians; and for these reasons do not deserve the confidence of the House of Commons.
It does not read correctly, Mr. Speaker, but I think what the hon. member meant was quite clear. It has always seemed to me that the serious speeches that have emanated from the northeast corner of this building have never been given the attention which they deserve. I know that the hon. gentlemen over there in that corner are serious minded men who study the writings of learned men who have thought out a way in which the world should be governed. They have thought this matter out and from time to time they have placed their ideas before us. Unfortunately most people do not take them very seriously. However, tonight I think I shall be justified in trying to analyse what the hon. member for Assiniboia meant. I do not think he gave the explanation in his speech or by the words which he has put into this subamendment.
I think that the key words in the subamendment-and these should be carefully noted by everyone-are "failure to promote the planned development of our resources". What is meant by "the planned development of our resources"? If you were speaking to a grade 8 child and you asked him what a plan meant, he would probably say, "Well, mother plans to take us to the movies on Saturday afternoon". But when you speak about a plan to the hon. member for Assiniboia or to his revered leader who led the C.C.F. party in Saskatchewan to victory for so many years, to them it means an entirely different thing. It means something that will affect the lives of everybody who comes under their sway or power.
Let us therefore look at this planned development of our resources and let us see what could be involved if we were to adopt this suggestion as a move towards settling the real problems confronting the country. The Leader of the Opposition had the good sense to say nothing in detail as to what should be done to improve things. He knows full well that this government has been doing a great many things which all hon. members in the opposition in both parties have supported. They have supported nearly every measure we brought in which has resulted in benefit to this country and has improved the trade of this country.
The Address-Hon. W. J. Browne
I remember reading a long time ago a statement by a writer who lived in a socialist country. He started out his book by saying, "Have nothing to do with planners". That left a great impression upon my mind and I should like to repeat what he said: "Have nothing to do with planners". What does that mean? These people are not going to be satisfied just with planning to bring about the right sort of climate in which industry can thrive and people can prosper. No, they want to plan everything. They want to plan not only the development of our resources but sound monetary, fiscal investment and trade policies.
Let us deal with monetary policies. Does it mean that they are going to take control of the banks and nationalize them, as the labour party wanted to do in Great Britain, nationalize both railways and do away with all sorts of private enterprise as the labour party did in Great Britain? The labour party of Great Britain went down to defeat ten years ago and it is very doubtful whether the British people will ever go back to the labour party again after the experience they had with them.
With respect to planned development, I suppose there was never a man in the history of Canada who had as good an opportunity to carry out a planned development of resources as did the premier of the province from which I come. In 1949 the present premier of Newfoundland was asked to form a government and he was a socialist. He was always a socialist as long as I knew him although he called himself a Liberal.
