The former leader, Mr. Coldwell, told me that. We know the definition of Mr. St. Laurent that socialists are only Liberals in a hurry, so when I say that the premier of Newfoundland was a socialist he could probably be described as a Liberal in a hurry.
When he came into office in 1949 he had the greatest opportunity that any man ever had to build up a sound and prosperous province because the public debt of the province of Newfoundland at that time was only $5 million. As a result of arrangements which had been made with the government of Canada, the public debt which was roughly about $70 million was reduced to about $5 million. In addition, there was a cash balance of about $42 million and assets which were

A year ago, it may be recalled, we on this side of the house, in our anxiety to see what the government proposed to do to alleviate the dreadful unemployment then at large in the country, gave up the right to participate in this debate. We left open to the government sufficient time so that they might, in lieu of the time taken on the debate on the speech from the throne, bring forward whatever massive program they had in order to assist the people of Canada.
Even those feeble assists given to the economy by this government in 1961 have borne some stunted fruit, but the Canadian people stand today, more than a year later, not much closer to the gates of economic heaven than they did at the time I first came into this house.
While it is true that unemployment is somewhat reduced and employment in Canada is higher, what of those thousands who remain without employment, so many of them out of work and out of benefits now for more than months, some for years? Is the government to


be content with the winter works program and its temporary survival training courses, these projects of little note and narrow impact? Are we in this country expected to be satisfied with these measures, in light of today's unemployment figures, in the same sense as the man who keeps beating himself over the head with a bat and who answers, when he is asked why, "Because it feels so good when I stop"?
What an indictment was given yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) of this past year of government by impulse. One would anticipate, with such major issues as our trade position, our long term employment policies, the ills of transportation, of immigration and the like left undecided after the longest session of our parliamentary history, that such a searching criticism as that levelled by the Leader of the Opposition would for once be met by a statesmanlike, carefully detailed answer of defence, if defence there be, of government policy.
Instead, we were treated once again to that far from unfamiliar action of the right hon. gentleman who now leads this government, a niggardly personal attack upon those in this party and its policies. Instead of attacking the problems of Canada the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) once again indicated that he is not equal to doing more than attack the Liberals of Canada. Once again he showed his contempt for parliament and the people. The people called for the solid bread of a clear, consistent policy of growth and expansion, for the impetus which can be given to a national economy by wise and steady leadership. In place of the bread for which they call they receive a crumbling cake demonstrating a cynical belief that once again the Canadian people can be bought off.
Where, in the debate which took place yesterday and this morning, did the Prime Minister show those great qualities of heart and mind demanded by people in these swiftly changing times? Instead, the right hon. gentleman lurched from point to point, once calling us the new Liberal party and then complaining that the same old people were within the party. And every now and then, with a glint in his eye for what he has shockingly called a servile press, he tossed out a piece of his crummy cake designed to take the country's eyes off his otherwise tasteless display.
To top it all off he had the temerity to say, as did the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) in yesterday's debate to be found at page 57 of Hansard, that the Leader of the Opposition was smearing this country. In fact, the Leader of the Opposition

attempted to state the facts as we on this side see them and as, indeed, it is our responsibility as members of the opposition to state them. He sought to bring these facts to the attention of the country and to the house. As for the accusation that he was smearing the country, I should like, with great respect, to read some of the things which the right hon. gentleman himself said in a debate which took place on March 15, 1955. I refer, first of all, to his words as reported at page 2035 of Hansard:
No one here wants to speak of depression. We on this side of the house hope the government will act, because there is no depression in other countries of the world. In Britain there is no such thing as serious unemployment today, the unemployment in Britain being less than half of our unemployment with a population several times greater than ours. The same condition prevails in West Germany and in other private enterprise countries.
Remember that this talk of a depression in 1955, this criticism of a government for its unemployment figures came from a man who now guides Canada's destiny and who has guided it into, but not out of, the greatest unemployment in our history. Then again, also as reported at page 2035, we find this passage:
We do not believe in preaching pessimism; we do not want to see the condition of affairs brought about which will create panic; but we are asking the government to act now.
That is what we on this side are doing. We are asking the government to act now. We are not smearing the Canadian people; we are not preaching doom and gloom. Our words amount to little more or less than those used by the right hon. gentleman who now calls them almost subversive.
There is a further quotation which I think hon. gentlemen should hear and it is to be found at page 2037. I ask hon. members to listen to it with great care bearing in mind that in the speech from the throne in 1960 there was a singular word which did not appear. That word was "unemployment". It does occur in the speech from the throne which was presented to us only a few days ago. But listen to what the then private hon. member for Prince Albert had to say as reported in Hansard:
The government does not even recognize that there is serious unemployment. Unless they do recognize that fact they cannot achieve in their minds any actuality for the solution of the problem.
This is from a man whose spokesman in the government later said: unemployment is not a serious condition in this country; it will go away with the snow. There is one further quotation to be found on the same page and these words were spoken by the same hon. gentleman:

Those who now sit in the seats of the mighty and who are responsible for such purple passages in the Hansard of that year are the same individuals who have been at the helm while unemployment has mounted and trade has slipped.
There is one final passage I should like to quote in which the hon. member for Prince Albert, as he then was, summed up the burden of his thinking. I, at this time, will make the same appeal as he did then:
Will the Prime Minister not assure the Canadian people that he believes action is necessary and that... one of the first things to which this conference will give consideration is the problem of unemployment? Will he not state that he realizes that if we continue to deliberately delude ourselves concerning the unemployment situation we shall bring about a fear complex in this country which will have serious results in the future?
So went the gloom of that day. This was from a man who at that time said he was speaking out for the benefit of Canada. Well, we on this side of the house speak out for the benefit of Canada. We on this side ask the government to recognize this problem, not to sit back in contentment because a few thousand more people are at work than were at work a year ago. We ask them to remember the hundreds of thousands of families in this country who tonight are still without an adequate income.
We have been subjected in this country to a series of numbing shocks-shocks so severe that our foes gloat, and our friends agonize over our future. First was the shock of that tidal wave of unemployment which rose and rose to subside only when seasonal workers might find spring employment. Three quarters of a million Canadians and their friends and relatives shivered without incomes, and others feared the deluge might catch them as well. Then, when all Canada began to draw a tentative breath and hope that unemployment might be easing, came the shock of the Coyne fiasco, as unholy a row as has ever been seen in this country and caused entirely by the refusal of this government, led by a self-styled defender of the rights of the individual, to permit one particular individual his day in court.

The Address-Miss LaMarsh
Then, we had the long delayed budget wherein the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) swallowed his tail without blinking. I have forgotten exactly what reptile this trick imitates. Surely, no minister has ever before so completely reversed himself, maintaining all along that his 1960 speeches respecting devaluating the Canadian dollar and his 1961 speeches say the same thing and that he was right both times.
Then, this strong right arm of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) went off on a trade jaunt to Ghana where, by careful leaks, he and his breezy cohort proceeded in a working conference to discuss the imminent entry of Britain into negotiations to join the common market. There, Mr. Speaker, we were treated to a neat switch on the old adage and these ministers conducted themselves there as though perhaps they were of the view, "If you can't join them, beat them." These two ministers who bear the responsibility for finance and trade and commerce have, by speeches from one part of the country to another, in all of their public utterances over a period of months, made clear that Canada by whining, wheedling, kicking or screaming or any show of petulance or anger, would make it clear that the British government might not, although duly elected to look after its own people, enter into such negotiations.
Well, we have lost now, Mr. Speaker, more than a year. We have lost now the original favoured position for discussing our entry into the Six. We have lost this impetus and we have gained nothing but world wide condemnation in this loss. We, in this country, but a few short years ago were thought of as being ably and well governed, but now we receive letters from those in and out of financial institutions, people from all parts of the world and particularly from England and the United States, asking us what it is that Canada proposes to do. What has happened to Canada? Why is it that she proceeds no longer in a calm and studied way? Why is it that she appears governed by impulse?
Then, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the chief cause of complaint, the complaint of all Canadians against this evil genius, as he has been called, this man who sits in the highest seat in this country, this man who must have-

speechtext: The suggestion has been made, and I think it not without substance, that the application of the term "evil genius" to a member of parliament is contrary to the practice and the rules. I suggest to the hon. lady that she might very well reconsider that expression.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, Your Honour; I was merely quoting what I had read elsewhere.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. lady probably appreciates that to adopt a quotation of others is to adopt the words themselves. I would not think that that modified the position.

speechtext: I do not know that my personal knowledge of the term is completely correct. I will bow to Your Honour's superior judgment in this regard and will desist from the use of the phrase.

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but it being 9:45 o'clock it is my duty, pursuant to section 3 of standing order 38 as provisionally amended, to interrupt these proceedings and put forthwith the question on any subamendment now before the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the house leader what we will do tomorrow and whether he has decided yet when the interruption of debate will come for the discussion of the matters which were referred to by the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We will continue this debate tomorrow, Mr. Speaker. At the conclusion of the sitting tomorrow I shall be able to inform the house with regard to the question asked by the hon. member.
